title: Enough Is a Number: What 49 Experiments Say About Protein
dek: The gym rules about protein sound like physics. The research says something more relaxed, and more useful: protein works like a threshold, not a dial.

blocks.text: Spend a week around any weight room and you will hear three rules repeated like laws of nature. Eat a gram of protein per pound of bodyweight. Get a shake down within thirty minutes of your last set or the workout is wasted. And don't bother eating more than thirty grams at once, because your body can't use it.

All three sound precise. All three sound like they came out of a lab. One of them is roughly right for a reason almost nobody who repeats it knows. The other two fall apart once you look at how they were tested.

The more interesting story isn't any single number. It's how a fuzzy range of evidence gets hardened into gym rules, and how the actual science, once you read it, points to an idea that applies far beyond nutrition: some inputs work like a volume knob, and some work like a light switch. Protein is much closer to a switch.
The floor, not the target

Start with the official number. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for protein in the US and Canada is **0.8 grams per kilogram of bodyweight per day**. For an 80 kg (about 176 lb) adult, that's 64 grams, roughly two chicken breasts' worth.

The RDA is often misread as a recommendation for everyone. It isn't designed for that. It's set to cover the basic needs of almost all healthy adults, meaning enough to avoid deficiency and maintain the tissue you already have. It was never meant to answer a different question: how much protein does someone need who is deliberately trying to build muscle?

It helps to know what protein is actually doing. Your muscles aren't static objects. They're constantly being taken apart and rebuilt, protein by protein, every hour of every day. Muscle grows only when building outpaces breakdown over weeks and months. Training is what tips that balance toward building; dietary protein provides the amino acids the rebuilding crew needs. Without the training signal, extra protein mostly gets burned for energy or used elsewhere.

To answer that one, you need experiments where people lift weights for weeks, some eat more protein and some don't, and researchers measure what happens to their muscle. Lots of those experiments exist. The problem is that most are small, and small studies bounce around. So in 2018 a team led by Robert Morton at McMaster University pooled them.
The study that pooled everything

Morton's group gathered every randomized controlled trial they could find that met two conditions: participants did resistance training for at least six weeks, and some of them got extra protein while others didn't. They ended up with **49 trials and 1,863 people**, published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine*. It remains one of the largest analyses of its kind.

items.label: Randomized studies pooled, with 1,863 participants
Average extra fat-free mass gained with added protein
Daily intake beyond which extra protein added no more muscle

blocks.source: Morton et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018

blocks.text: Two results matter. The first is that extra protein did help. People who supplemented gained more strength (about 2.5 kg more on their one-rep max) and more fat-free mass than those who didn't. The second is how *much* it helped: an average of **0.30 kg** of extra fat-free mass over the course of the studies. That's real, and it adds up over years, but it's about two-thirds of a pound. Training did the heavy lifting. Protein topped it off.

There were also two telling patterns. The benefit shrank as people got older, and it was larger in people who already had lifting experience. Younger, trained lifters got the most out of extra protein, which makes sense: they're the ones whose training is pushing hardest against the limits of their materials.
Where the curve goes flat

The most cited part of the paper is a break-point analysis. The researchers plotted each study group's total daily protein intake against how much fat-free mass it gained. Gains rose with protein up to about **1.62 g/kg per day**, and above that the line went flat. More protein, no more muscle.

Here's the part that usually gets left out. The uncertainty around that number is wide: the 95% confidence interval runs from **1.03 to 2.20 g/kg**. The break-point model itself didn't quite reach statistical significance (p = 0.079). The authors were upfront about this, and because of that uncertainty they suggested that people who want to be sure of maximizing gains could aim for about 2.2 g/kg, the top of the range.

blocks.title: Daily protein for an 80 kg (176 lb) adult
blocks.note: Multipliers from the meta-analysis applied to an 80 kg body; 2.2 g/kg is the top of the plateau's 95% confidence interval.
blocks.source: Morton et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018

blocks.text: Remember too that a plateau in pooled data is an average across hundreds of people. Some individuals will top out lower, some higher. That's exactly why a range is more honest than a single magic number, and why the sensible move is to aim somewhere inside it rather than argue about the second decimal place.

Now the gym rule makes sense. One gram per pound is 2.2 grams per kilogram. It isn't the amount most people need; it's the conservative top of the range. It works, but mostly because it overshoots. If you hit 1.6 g/kg consistently, you're already at the point where, on average, extra protein stopped producing extra muscle in the pooled data.

Think of protein as building materials and training as the work order. Below a certain amount, a shortage of bricks slows the job. Above it, piling more bricks on the site doesn't make the crew build faster. The work order is what sets the pace.
The anabolic window that wasn't

The thirty-minute window is a more instructive case, because it shows how a myth can be born from honest research. Early studies compared people who drank a protein shake right after training with people who drank nothing. The shake group often did better, and the conclusion was that *timing* mattered.

But look at what actually differed between the groups. The shake group didn't just eat protein at a particular time. They ate *more protein, total*. Timing and total amount were tangled together, so there was no way to tell which one was doing the work.

In 2013, Brad Schoenfeld, Alan Aragon and James Krieger untangled them. They pooled 23 studies on muscle growth covering 525 people and used a statistical model that accounted for each study's total protein intake. A simple pooled analysis did show a small benefit for timing. Once total protein was controlled for, the effect of timing disappeared. The strongest predictor of muscle growth was simply how much protein people ate across the day.

That's a useful mental move to keep in your pocket for any health claim. When someone says X causes Y, ask what else was different between the people who did X and the people who didn't. Often the hidden variable is doing all the work.
The thirty-gram ceiling

The idea that your body can only use around 25 to 30 grams at a sitting has a real origin too. Short-term studies measure muscle protein synthesis, the rate at which muscle builds new protein, over a few hours after a meal. In those windows, synthesis rises with dose and then levels off around that range.

A 2013 study by José Areta and colleagues tested how to spread protein across a day. Trained men did a leg workout, then drank 80 grams of whey over 12 hours in one of three patterns: eight 10 g doses, four 20 g doses, or two 40 g doses. The middle pattern, **20 grams every three hours**, produced the highest synthesis rates. That's a decent argument for spreading protein across several meals.

But a ceiling on how fast you build in a short window isn't the same as a ceiling on how much you can use. In 2023, Jorn Trommelen and colleagues in the Netherlands gave people either 25 grams or 100 grams of protein after a workout and tracked where it went using multiple isotope tracers. The 100-gram dose produced a bigger anabolic response that lasted **more than 12 hours**, and very little of the extra was burned off as fuel. The body didn't waste it. It just processed it more slowly.

blocks.title: Gym rules vs the evidence

left.head: What you hear
items: Eat 1 g per pound or you won't grow
Shake within 30 minutes or the session is wasted
Over 30 g in one meal is wasted
Protein builds muscle

right.head: What the research shows
items: Gains flattened around 1.6 g/kg (0.7 g/lb); 1 g/lb is a safe overshoot
Total daily intake predicted growth; timing didn't once total was controlled
Large doses are used, just more slowly
Training builds muscle; protein supplies the materials

blocks.text: A caveat on both of those studies: they measured synthesis rates for hours, not muscle size over months. They tell you about mechanisms, not final outcomes. The honest practical summary is that spreading protein across three to five meals is sensible and convenient, and a big protein-heavy dinner after a long day isn't wasted.

The same goes for the popular advice to eat protein before bed. A 2023 trial gave young men 45 grams of casein, 45 grams of whey, or a placebo before sleep after an evening workout. Both proteins raised overnight synthesis compared with placebo, and the expensive slow-digesting casein did no better than whey. It's a reasonable way to fit in another protein feeding. It isn't a secret weapon.
Turning it into meals

Converted to pounds, the plateau is about **0.7 grams per pound**. For a 165 lb person, that's roughly 115 to 120 grams a day. Eaten over four meals, that's about 30 grams each, which is a can of tuna, three or four eggs plus a glass of milk, a chicken breast, or a cup of Greek yogurt with something else on the side.

blocks.title: Setting your own number
items: Find your weight in kilograms (pounds divided by 2.2).
Multiply by 1.6 for your daily target; use up to 2.2 if you want a margin of safety.
Divide by the number of meals you actually eat, usually three to five.
Anchor every meal with one clear protein source before filling in the rest.
Check your intake honestly for a week, then stop counting and keep the pattern.

blocks.text: Notice what isn't on that list: powder. In the Morton analysis, supplements helped because they raised people's total intake, not because there's anything special about protein that comes in a tub. Powder is a convenience food. If the galley serves eggs at breakfast and meat at dinner, and you add milk, yogurt or jerky in between, you can get there without it. If a shake is the easiest way to close a gap during a long watch rotation, that's fine too. It's food, not magic.

One situation where aiming toward the top of the range makes extra sense is when you're eating less than you burn, for example while trying to lean out before a deployment. A calorie deficit makes the body more willing to break down muscle along with fat, and sports nutrition researchers commonly suggest higher protein during those phases to help hold on to what you've built. Combined with continued lifting, it's one of the simplest ways to make sure the weight you lose is mostly fat.

Two practical notes. First, these intakes are common in studies of healthy adults, but if you have kidney disease or another medical condition, talk to a doctor or your corpsman before raising protein a lot. Second, the age finding cuts both ways. Older adults respond less to protein, which is one more reason muscle built in your twenties is worth having: it's the account you'll be drawing on for decades.
The real lesson: find the bottleneck

Protein is a nice example of a common trap. People pour energy into the variable that's easiest to buy and measure, such as grams, timing, brands and windows, and comparatively little into the variable that drives results. In every one of those 49 trials, the participants were training consistently. That was the signal. Protein only mattered because it supported the signal.

Gamers will recognize the pattern. Once your frame rate is above what your monitor can display, buying a faster graphics card doesn't make you aim better. Below that point, hardware is a real handicap; above it, the limiting factor is practice. Protein is the frame rate. Get it high enough that it isn't holding you back, then stop shopping and start training.

Once you understand that protein behaves like a threshold, the strategy changes. You don't need to optimize it forever. You need to get to *enough*, make that automatic, and then spend your attention on the things with no ceiling in sight: showing up, adding weight or reps over time, and sleeping. Enough is a number. Find it, hit it, and move on to the hard part.

takeaways: About 1.6 g of protein per kg per day (0.7 g/lb) is where muscle gains flattened in the pooled data; 2.2 g/kg is a safe upper target.
The RDA of 0.8 g/kg prevents deficiency; it isn't designed for building muscle.
Total daily protein matters far more than timing. There's no 30-minute deadline.
Big protein meals aren't wasted, but spreading protein over 3–5 meals is easy and sensible.
Protein supplies materials; consistent hard training is what actually builds muscle.

title: The 500 Calories Nobody Decided to Eat
dek: Twenty people lived inside a federal research hospital for a month so scientists could answer a simple question: does processing itself change how much we eat?

blocks.text: For one month, twenty adults lived at the Clinical Center of the US National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland. They weren't sick. They were volunteers in an experiment designed to answer a question that nutrition science had argued about for years without a clean test: does the *processing* of food, separate from its sugar, salt, fat or fiber, change how much people eat?

For two weeks, their meals were built mostly from ultra-processed foods. For the other two weeks, their meals were built from unprocessed or minimally processed foods. The order was randomized. The rule for both diets was the same: eat as much or as little as you want.

On the ultra-processed diet, people ate about **500 more calories a day**. Not because anyone told them to, and not because they rated the food as tastier. They simply ate more, and they gained weight. Then, on the other diet, they ate less and lost it. It's one of the cleanest demonstrations we have that our food environment can make decisions for us that we never consciously make.
What counts as ultra-processed

Almost everything we eat is processed in some way. Milk is pasteurized, rice is milled, beans are dried and canned. So the term needs a sharper definition, and the most widely used one comes from a system called **NOVA**, developed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in Brazil. NOVA sorts food not by nutrients but by the extent and purpose of the industrial processing behind it.

blocks.title: The NOVA scale, from least to most processed
items: Unprocessed or minimally processed: fresh or frozen fruit and vegetables, eggs, plain meat, milk, rice, dried beans.
Processed culinary ingredients: oils, butter, sugar, salt, used to cook the first group.
Processed foods: simple combinations of the first two, like canned vegetables, cheese, cured meat or fresh bread.
Ultra-processed foods: industrial formulations built from refined substances and additives, like soda, packaged snacks, sweetened cereals and many ready meals.

blocks.text: The fourth group is the interesting one. Monteiro's team describes these as products assembled from substances extracted or modified from whole foods, often with ingredients you would rarely find in a home kitchen: high-fructose corn syrup, hydrogenated oils, protein isolates, and cosmetic additives like flavorings, emulsifiers and colorings. They're designed to be cheap, shelf-stable, convenient and very easy to like.
A useful rule of thumb from the NOVA researchers: if the ingredient list contains things you wouldn't recognize as food you could buy and cook with, it's probably in group four.
The experiment

The NIH study was led by Kevin Hall, a physicist turned metabolism researcher known for running tightly controlled feeding studies. The design had one especially clever feature. Hall's team worked to match the two diets on the things nutrition debates usually focus on. The meals offered were designed to be matched for calories, energy density, protein, carbs, fat, sugar, sodium and fiber. The main thing left to differ was how processed the food was.

The ten men and ten women, with an average age of about 31, were offered meals and snacks totaling about twice the calories each person needed to maintain their weight. Staff weighed what was left on every plate, so researchers knew exactly what each person ate. Body weight and other measures were tracked throughout.

items.label: Extra calories eaten per day on the ultra-processed diet
Average weight gained in two weeks on that diet
Average weight lost in two weeks on the unprocessed diet

blocks.source: Hall et al., Cell Metabolism, 2019

blocks.text: The extra calories came almost entirely from carbohydrate and fat. Protein intake barely moved: about two calories a day of difference, which is statistically nothing. And weight changes tracked intake closely, a strong sign the effect was real rather than a quirk of water or measurement.

blocks.title: Where the extra calories came from
blocks.note: Protein intake did not differ meaningfully between the two diets (about −2 kcal/day).
blocks.source: Hall et al., Cell Metabolism, 2019

blocks.text: Two more details are worth noticing. First, people rated the meals on both diets as about equally pleasant. The ultra-processed food wasn't simply more delicious. Second, people ate the ultra-processed meals noticeably faster, about **17 more calories per minute**. Soft, easy-to-chew food goes down quickly, and fullness signals from the gut take time to reach the brain.

There was a biological echo of this, too. On the unprocessed diet, blood levels of PYY, a gut hormone that suppresses appetite, went up, and ghrelin, a hormone that drives hunger, went down compared with baseline. The body seemed to be signaling more satisfaction from the less processed food, even though people's own ratings didn't register the difference.
Nobody in the study felt like they were overeating. Their hunger and fullness ratings were similar on both diets. The extra 500 calories happened below the level of conscious choice.
Why it might happen
The study showed *that* processing changed intake. It didn't prove exactly *why*. Hall and his colleagues discussed several candidate explanations, and they aren't mutually exclusive.

items: **Eating speed.** Food that requires little chewing gets eaten before satiety signals catch up.
**Protein leverage.** One theory says people keep eating until they hit a protein target; if protein comes diluted among refined carbs and fat, you overshoot calories getting there.
**Engineered combinations.** Many products pair fat, sugar, salt and refined starch in ways rarely found in whole foods, which may encourage overconsumption.
**Gut-brain signaling.** Refined, pre-broken-down food may trigger weaker fullness signals than intact food that digests slowly.

blocks.text: One detail complicates the clean story, and Hall's paper says so directly. The two diets were matched for energy density when drinks were included, but the ultra-processed diet relied on diet sodas to get there. Looking only at the solid food, the ultra-processed meals were about **85% more energy-dense**, meaning more calories packed into each bite. The authors think that likely contributed to the overeating. So part of what makes ultra-processed food easy to overeat may simply be that it's calorie-dense and quick to eat, which raises the question of whether processing is the cause or just a marker for those features.

There was also a sobering practical finding. Using prices from a local supermarket, the team estimated that a week of ultra-processed meals at 2,000 calories a day cost about **$106 in ingredients**, versus about **$151** for the unprocessed version. Ultra-processed food is cheaper and quicker, which goes a long way toward explaining why it dominates.
How much of our food it is

Dominates is not an exaggeration. In 2025, the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics reported that from August 2021 to August 2023, ultra-processed foods made up **55% of calories** eaten by Americans aged one and older. For young people aged 1 to 18 it was nearly 62%; for adults, 53%.

blocks.title: Share of calories from ultra-processed food, US
blocks.note: Data from August 2021 to August 2023.
blocks.source: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief 536, 2025

blocks.text: The biggest single sources were sandwiches including burgers, followed by sweet bakery products, salty snacks and sweetened drinks. In other words, for most Americans, ultra-processed food isn't an occasional treat. It's the main source of energy.

Large observational studies have linked diets high in ultra-processed food with worse health. A 2024 umbrella review in the *BMJ* pulled together 45 pooled analyses covering nearly 10 million people and found higher ultra-processed food intake associated with a higher risk of 32 of the 45 health outcomes examined, including heart disease deaths, type 2 diabetes, anxiety and depression.

The honest caveat is important. These are associations, not experiments. People who eat a lot of ultra-processed food differ in many other ways, such as income, sleep, stress and exercise, and those differences are hard to fully control for. The review's own quality grading rated most of the evidence as low or very low quality. The signal is consistent, but observational data can't by itself prove cause.
The newer test

That's why controlled trials matter, and Hall's 2019 study had real limits: twenty people, two weeks per diet, in a hospital. In 2025 a larger and longer trial in England, published in *Nature Medicine*, asked a sharper question. What if both diets follow official healthy-eating guidelines, and the only difference is processing?

Fifty-five adults each spent eight weeks on a minimally processed diet and eight weeks on an ultra-processed one, with both built to fit the UK's Eatwell Guide. The ultra-processed version used reformulated, nutritionally improved products such as breakfast cereals, ready meals and plant-based alternatives, many carrying health claims on the label. All the food was delivered to participants' homes in its normal branded packaging, and they ate as much as they liked.

That design matters. Earlier trials, including Hall's, took place in hospital wards, which are about as far from real life as eating gets. Here people ate at home, at work and with their families, much as they normally would, just with someone else doing the shopping.

items.label: Body weight change on the minimally processed diet (8 weeks)
Body weight change on the ultra-processed diet (8 weeks)

blocks.source: Dicken et al., Nature Medicine, 2025

blocks.text: People lost weight on both diets, likely because both were healthier than what they usually ate. But they lost about twice as much on the minimally processed version. The gap was modest, and the trial was still small. Yet it points the same direction as Hall's: even when the nutrient numbers look good on paper, how food is made seems to matter.
The critics have a point too

Not every scientist is convinced that ultra-processed is the right category. NOVA lumps together foods with very different nutritional profiles: a packaged wholegrain bread and a can of soda can sit in the same group. Some studies find that certain ultra-processed foods, such as some breads, cereals and yogurts, aren't linked to worse outcomes at all. Critics argue that the real culprits may be specific features, like energy density, eating speed or particular combinations of ingredients, rather than processing as such.

Hall's own paper acknowledged that the NOVA system has been criticized as too imprecise to base dietary advice on, even as Brazil's national dietary guidelines use it to advise people to avoid ultra-processed food. Two serious groups of experts looking at the same evidence can reasonably land in different places about what the category means.

That debate is healthy, and it's ongoing. Researchers are now trying to separate out which features of ultra-processed food drive overeating. The answer will probably end up more specific than the category itself.
What to do with this

None of this calls for food purity or guilt. On a submarine especially, a lot of the food is processed out of necessity: it has to survive months of storage. The goal isn't zero ultra-processed food. It's noticing that some foods quietly push your intake up, and adjusting where it's easy.

A few moves follow directly from the evidence. Build meals around foods that look like what they are: eggs, meat, fish, rice, potatoes, beans, fruit, vegetables, milk. Eat a little slower, especially with soft, easy foods. Get protein in every meal so you're not chasing it through snacks. And be aware that the bag of chips during a long watch isn't a moral failure; it's simply food that's engineered to be easy to keep eating.

It also helps to think in swaps rather than bans. Oatmeal instead of a frosted cereal some mornings. A sandwich built from sliced meat and bread rather than a breaded, pre-fried patty. Nuts, fruit, cheese or a hard-boiled egg as watch snacks instead of something from a crinkly bag. Water or milk instead of soda most of the time. None of these changes is dramatic, and that's the point. Based on what the trials found, the effect of processing works through many small, unnoticed differences in how much gets eaten, so the fix can work the same way.

And if a meal is mostly ultra-processed, because that's what's on the menu tonight, you can still apply the eating-speed lesson. Put the fork down between bites, drink some water, and give your gut a few extra minutes to report back before going for seconds.

The bigger idea is about agency. We like to think every bite is a decision. Hall's volunteers weren't trying to overeat, didn't feel like they were, and didn't find the food more delicious. They ate 500 extra calories a day anyway. The lesson isn't that willpower is useless. It's that the smartest place to apply it is upstream, in what you put on the plate and in reach, rather than downstream, in a fight with every individual bite.

takeaways: In a tightly controlled NIH trial, people ate about 500 more calories a day on an ultra-processed diet without trying to.
The diets were matched on sugar, fat, sodium and fiber, so processing itself seemed to drive the difference.
Ultra-processed food supplies about 55% of calories in the US.
Observational links to disease are consistent but mostly low-quality evidence; the trials are small but point the same way.
Build meals around recognizable whole foods, eat a bit slower, and shape your environment rather than fighting every bite.

title: Forty-Nine Days Without the Sun
dek: Your skin makes a hormone out of a narrow band of ultraviolet light. Here is what happens when you take that light away, and what the biggest trials say about replacing it with a pill.

blocks.text: In a study published in 2005, Navy researchers described drawing blood from 51 sailors before their submarine left on a 76-day deployment. Half got a daily vitamin D pill; half got a placebo. Then the boat went under, and the sampling continued: on day 49, again on day 55, and once more when the boat came home.

Both groups lost vitamin D while submerged, the pill group included. But the most striking detail sits in between the blood draws. Around day 49 the crew got a six-day liberty period in Pearl Harbor. When the sailors came back aboard, their levels had climbed back to roughly where they started. The authors put it plainly: six days of sunlight made up for 49 days without it.

That one result says a lot about vitamin D. It is not really a vitamin in the usual sense, something you mostly have to eat. It is something your body manufactures, and the factory runs on sunlight. A submarine is about the purest experiment there is in shutting that factory down.
Your skin is a factory

Vitamin D production starts with a cholesterol-like molecule in your skin. When ultraviolet B light, the slice of sunlight between about 290 and 315 nanometers, hits it, the molecule is split and rearranged into previtamin D3, which slowly settles into vitamin D3. That is the raw material. Your liver converts it into **25-hydroxyvitamin D**, the storage form and the number a blood test reports. Your kidneys convert a small amount of that into the active hormone, which helps your gut absorb calcium and keeps your bones mineralized.

blocks.title: From sunlight to working hormone
items: UVB light (about 290–315 nm) reaches the skin
A cholesterol-like molecule in the skin becomes previtamin D3, then vitamin D3
The liver turns D3 into 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the form a blood test measures
The kidneys convert some of it into the active hormone
The active hormone helps the gut absorb calcium for bones and muscles

blocks.text: The catch is that UVB is fussy. It is the part of sunlight most easily blocked by the atmosphere, so the sun's angle matters enormously. In a classic 1988 experiment, researchers exposed skin samples to cloudless winter sun in Boston and found that from November through February, it produced **no** previtamin D3 at all. In Edmonton, Canada, further north, the dead season ran from October through March. Further south the factory kept running all winter.

Ordinary window glass blocks most UVB, and indoor lighting is not designed to emit it, so you can sit under bright lights all day and make essentially nothing. Seen this way, a submarine on patrol is a permanent vitamin D winter. So is a windowless office, a night-shift job, or a gaming room with blackout curtains. The boat is just the most extreme version of how a lot of people already live.
What a patrol actually does
The Duplessis study gives the cleanest picture of the decline. The supplement in that study was 400 IU a day, a small dose by modern standards, and it was not enough to hold levels steady.

blocks.title: Blood vitamin D before and during a submerged patrol
blocks.note: Both groups fell during the first submerged stretch; a 6-day port call then brought levels back near baseline.
blocks.source: Duplessis et al., Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine, 2005

blocks.text: Other studies complicate the story in useful ways. A 2014 trial on a three-month US submarine patrol found that **49%** of the crew were already below 50 nmol/L before the boat even left. Surprisingly, average levels rose slightly in every group during that patrol, including placebo, and the 2,000 IU group rose most, by about 13 nmol/L. The researchers found the change depended heavily on where each sailor started and on body mass. A Royal Navy study published in 2017 found the opposite pattern among non-supplementing submariners: levels fell, and in winter deployers they ended up notably below 25 nmol/L, while sailors who took supplements finished far higher.

Why would levels rise on one patrol and fall on another? The researchers could not say for certain, and it is worth resisting a neat story. Where a crew starts matters, since people who begin very low tend to respond more to any given intake. The season they left in matters, because a sailor who departs after a sunny summer is carrying a bigger reserve than one who departs in February. Diet aboard, body size and whether anyone was quietly taking their own supplements all add noise. Small studies on single boats are good at showing that something can happen, and weak at showing how often it does.

A 2023 systematic review pulled together nine submarine studies covering 305 male submariners on patrols of 30 to 92 days. Its conclusion was that low vitamin D is common across the Navy and especially among submariners, though the studies were too different from one another to combine into a single number. The honest summary: going under does not guarantee a crash, but many sailors start low, and the boat removes the one source that would normally fix it.
How much is enough?

Here is where people get confused, partly because two units float around. US labs usually report ng/mL; much of the research uses nmol/L. To convert, multiply ng/mL by about 2.5. So 20 ng/mL is 50 nmol/L.

In 2011 the Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine) reviewed the evidence and set the numbers most US guidance still uses. They were deliberately built on the assumption of minimal sun exposure, which makes them unusually relevant to life underwater.

items.label: Daily RDA for ages 1–70
Blood level (50 nmol/L) that meets the needs of 97.5% of people
Tolerable upper intake level for adults

blocks.source: Ross et al., Institute of Medicine DRI report summary, 2011

blocks.text: The committee also made a point that gets lost in the supplement aisle: they concluded the share of people with inadequate vitamin D in North America had been *overestimated*, partly because some labs flagged anyone under 30 ng/mL as deficient. National survey data from 2011 to 2014 put about **5%** of Americans at risk of deficiency (under 30 nmol/L) and about **18%** at risk of inadequacy (30 to 49 nmol/L). Notably, the deficiency risk peaked in adults aged 20 to 39 and was much higher among Black Americans, whose darker skin makes vitamin D more slowly from the same sun.
The miracle vitamin that wasn't

For about two decades vitamin D looked like a wonder nutrient. Study after study found that people with low blood levels had more heart disease, cancer, depression, infections, diabetes and early death. The obvious move was to give people vitamin D and watch those diseases fall.

That is not what happened. A 2014 review in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology* looked at 290 prospective cohort studies and 172 randomized trials. The observational studies showed strong links; the trials mostly showed no benefit. The authors' interpretation was blunt: low vitamin D looks more like a *marker* of poor health than a cause of it. Sick people spend more time indoors, and inflammation itself can lower blood levels. The number on the lab report was a symptom, not the disease.

blocks.title: Why the early research misled everyone

left.head: Observational studies
items: Compare people who happen to have high or low levels
Low vitamin D tracks with illness, inactivity and time indoors
Can't tell which came first
Showed big apparent benefits

right.head: Randomized trials
items: Randomly assign vitamin D or placebo
Cancel out lifestyle differences
Test cause, not correlation
Mostly found little or no benefit in people with normal levels

blocks.text: The biggest test was the VITAL trial: 25,871 US adults randomly assigned to 2,000 IU a day or placebo for a median of 5.3 years. Vitamin D did not significantly reduce invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events. A follow-up analysis of the same people found it did not reduce fractures either. Those were healthy adults who were not selected for being low, which is exactly the point: topping up people who already have enough does little.

Respiratory infections are the most interesting case, because the effect has shrunk as more data arrived. A 2017 analysis of 25 trials found a modest protective effect. A 2021 update with far more trials found a smaller one. A 2025 update with over 61,000 participants found the effect was no longer statistically significant.

blocks.title: Vitamin D and respiratory infections: the shrinking effect
blocks.note: 1.0 means no effect. Lower is better. The 2025 estimate's uncertainty range includes 1.0.
blocks.source: Martineau et al., BMJ, 2017; Jolliffe et al., Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, 2021 and 2025

blocks.text: In 2024 the Endocrine Society folded all of this into a guideline. It suggested *against* taking vitamin D above the recommended intake for healthy adults under 75 just to lower disease risk, and against routine blood testing for the general population. It still suggested supplements for children, people over 75, pregnancy and high-risk prediabetes.
The reframe: a gap-filler, not a power-up

Put the submarine studies next to the big trials and a clear idea emerges. Vitamin D behaves less like a performance enhancer and more like a fuel gauge. Below a threshold, things go wrong: bones can't mineralize properly, and the people most deficient seem to get the most out of a fix. Above it, more does not seem to buy you much.

That changes the useful question. It is not "should I take a lot of vitamin D?" It is "am I likely to be on the wrong side of the line?" Most people living normal lives are not. Someone who spends months at a time with zero UVB, who may have started low, and who might have darker skin or a winter homeport, is a much more reasonable candidate. The trials that found nothing were mostly testing people who were never short in the first place.

It also helps to understand what "low" actually costs you. The well-established damage is to bone. When vitamin D runs short for a long time, the gut absorbs less calcium, the body pulls calcium from the skeleton to keep blood levels steady, and in severe, prolonged cases adult bone can soften, a condition called osteomalacia that shows up as aches, tenderness and muscle weakness. That is the territory where the evidence is solid. The long list of other benefits once promised for vitamin D is where it has mostly fallen apart.

One more useful mental model: your blood level is a *stock*, not a flow. Because vitamin D is stored in fat and the storage form lingers in the blood for weeks, what you did over the last couple of months matters far more than what you did yesterday. That is why a long patrol drains it slowly instead of all at once, why a short port call can rebuild a surprising amount, and why a steady daily habit beats an occasional giant dose. It is closer to a savings account than a fuel tank you top off each morning.
The pattern in the research: vitamin D fixes a shortage well and does little for people who already have enough. Your job is to figure out which group you are in, not to chase the highest number.
What to actually do

Treat this as a conversation to have with your corpsman or medical department, not a prescription. Individual needs vary, some medical conditions and medications change the picture, and the Navy may have its own guidance for deployed crews. With that said, the evidence points to a few sensible moves.

items: **Use your liberty.** The Duplessis data suggest that a few days of real sun can rebuild a lot of what weeks underwater took away. Midday sun in spring and summer works best; get some exposure without burning.
**Eat the few foods that have it.** Fatty fish like salmon and sardines, egg yolks and fortified milk or cereal all contribute, though food alone rarely covers it.

**If you supplement, stay in the boring range.** Doses around the RDA, and well under the 4,000 IU upper limit, are what the guidelines support unless a clinician advises otherwise. More is not better.
**Ask about testing if you have a reason.** Long patrols, a history of low levels, frequent stress fractures or bone pain are reasons to bring it up. Routine testing for everyone isn't recommended.

blocks.text: One more reason to avoid megadoses: vitamin D is fat-soluble, so your body stores it rather than flushing the excess. True toxicity is rare and usually comes from taking extremely high doses for a long time, but when it happens it raises blood calcium and can cause vomiting, confusion and kidney problems. The fix for a shortage is modest and steady, not heroic.

The deeper lesson reaches beyond one vitamin. A correlation between a blood marker and good health is a hint, not an instruction. Vitamin D looked like a cure for everything because healthy, active, outdoor people had more of it. The sun was doing double duty, and the pill could only copy half the job.

takeaways: Your skin makes vitamin D from UVB light; indoor light and window glass provide essentially none, so a patrol is a long vitamin D winter.
In one Navy study, six days of liberty sunlight restored what 49 days submerged had taken.
Big trials found vitamin D doesn't prevent cancer, heart disease or fractures in people who already have enough.
It works best as a gap-filler: the question is whether you're low, not how high you can go.
Stay within recommended doses and talk to your corpsman before supplementing or testing.

title: You Breathe Your Fat Out
dek: When you lose ten kilograms of fat, more than eight of them leave through your lungs. Most doctors and trainers asked about it got the answer wrong.

blocks.text: Here's a question that sounds easy until you try to answer it. When someone loses ten kilograms of fat, where do the ten kilograms actually go? Not where the *energy* goes. Where the *stuff* goes, the atoms that used to sit under the skin and now don't.

Most people say it gets burned off as energy, or turned into heat. Some say it leaves as waste in the toilet. Some say it turns into muscle. In 2014, two Australian researchers put the question to 150 doctors, dietitians and personal trainers. More than half said the fat was converted into energy or heat.
That answer is wrong, and the right one is stranger and more satisfying. Most of the mass of the fat you lose leaves your body through your mouth, as carbon dioxide, one invisible breath at a time.
A physicist asks a simple question

The story starts with Ruben Meerman, an Australian physicist and science communicator who lost about 15 kilograms in 2013. Being a physicist, he wanted to know where it had gone. He couldn't find a clear answer in textbooks or from experts, so he worked it out with Andrew Brown, a biochemist at the University of New South Wales. Their short paper in the *BMJ* in December 2014 has been one of the most widely shared nutrition explanations ever since.

The other popular answers fail for simpler reasons. Fat doesn't become muscle: they're different tissues made of different molecules, and one can't be converted into the other any more than a gas tank can turn into an engine. And very little of the fat you lose leaves in the toilet. Solid waste is mostly undigested food, bacteria and water, not the contents of your fat cells.

The reason so many professionals answered wrong is a mix-up between energy and matter. Nutrition is usually taught in calories, which are units of energy. We say fat gets burned, which sounds like it vanishes in a flash. But energy and mass are different accounts. When fat is used for fuel, the body does release energy, which powers your muscles and keeps you warm. The atoms that held that energy don't disappear. They have to leave in some physical form.

If you've studied reactor physics, you know that in fission a measurable sliver of mass turns into energy. In chemistry, including the chemistry in your cells, that mass change is far too tiny to matter. For practical purposes, every atom of fat you lose is still an atom, and it has to exit somewhere.
The chemistry of a disappearing waistline

Body fat is stored mainly as *triglycerides*: molecules made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Meerman and Brown used a typical triglyceride with the formula C55H104O6, meaning 55 carbon atoms, 104 hydrogen atoms and 6 oxygen atoms. To completely break one down for fuel, your cells combine it with oxygen from the air you breathe.

When the reaction is finished, one triglyceride plus 78 molecules of oxygen becomes 55 molecules of carbon dioxide and 52 molecules of water, plus energy. You can check the bookkeeping: every carbon ends up in carbon dioxide, every hydrogen ends up in water, and the oxygen atoms are split between the two.

It's worth pausing on why fat is such a good fuel in the first place. Compared with sugars, fat molecules carry lots of carbon and hydrogen and very little oxygen. In chemical terms, they're barely oxidized yet, which means there's a lot of oxidizing left to do, and every step of it releases energy. That's why the body uses fat for long-term storage: it packs far more energy into each gram than carbohydrate does, so you can carry weeks of reserve fuel without hauling around enormous bulk.

The researchers then followed every atom. All the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. The hydrogen leaves as water. The fat's own oxygen atoms divide between the two products. Add up the masses, and the answer drops out: **84% of the fat's mass is exhaled as carbon dioxide**, and the remaining **16% becomes water**, which leaves as urine, sweat, breath moisture, tears and other fluids.

blocks.title: Where 10 kg of lost fat goes
blocks.note: Water exits through urine, sweat, breath, tears and other fluids.
blocks.source: Meerman & Brown, BMJ, 2014

blocks.text: The full exchange is even more striking. Oxidizing 10 kilograms of fat requires breathing in **29 kilograms of oxygen**. The process produces **28 kilograms of carbon dioxide** and **11 kilograms of water**. The oxygen you inhale to lose the fat weighs nearly three times as much as the fat itself.

items.label: Oxygen inhaled to fully oxidize 10 kg of fat
Carbon dioxide produced and exhaled
Water produced

blocks.source: Meerman & Brown, BMJ, 2014

blocks.text: The journey of a fat molecule
Knowing the start and end points, it's worth following the path in between, because it shows why fat loss is a whole-body process rather than something that happens to one spot.

blocks.title: From fat cell to exhaled breath
items: When the body needs more energy than it's getting from food, hormonal signals tell fat cells to release stored fuel.
Inside the fat cell, each triglyceride is split into glycerol and three fatty acids.
The fatty acids travel through the bloodstream to cells that need fuel, especially muscle.
Inside mitochondria, fatty acids are chopped into two-carbon pieces and fed into the Krebs cycle, which strips off carbon as CO2.
Hydrogen from the fuel combines with the oxygen you breathed in to form water, releasing the energy that makes ATP.
The CO2 dissolves into your blood, travels to your lungs and leaves with your next breath.

blocks.text: A few things follow from this path. First, fat leaves its storage cells and goes wherever fuel is needed. The working muscle doesn't pull fat from the fat directly on top of it. It draws from the bloodstream, which is supplied from fat stored all over the body.

That's why spot reduction doesn't work. In a 2011 study, 24 sedentary adults were randomized either to do seven abdominal exercises, two sets of ten reps, five days a week for six weeks, or to do nothing extra. The ab group got much better at curl-ups. Their belly fat, waist measurements and skinfolds didn't change compared with the control group. Training a muscle makes the muscle stronger. It doesn't empty the fat cells next to it.

Where fat comes off first, and last, is largely out of your hands. It depends on genetics, sex, hormones and age, which is why two people following the same plan can change shape in very different orders. The part you control is the overall balance. Keep that tilted the right way for long enough, and the stubborn areas get drawn down eventually, because the bloodstream doesn't play favorites forever.
Fat cells shrink, but they stay

A second surprise concerns the fat cells themselves. When you lose fat, you lose the *contents* of fat cells, not usually the cells. In a 2008 study in *Nature*, Kirsty Spalding and colleagues in Sweden used an extraordinary natural experiment to measure how fat cells come and go: traces of carbon-14 released into the atmosphere by Cold War nuclear bomb tests, which ended up in the DNA of cells formed during that era.

Here's how that works. Above-ground nuclear tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere. After the 1963 treaty that banned atmospheric testing, levels fell steadily year by year. Every cell copies its DNA when it's born, using carbon from food that came, ultimately, from the air of that year. So the carbon-14 level locked in a cell's DNA works like a date stamp, telling researchers roughly when that cell was formed.

They found that the number of fat cells in adults stays remarkably constant, even after major weight loss, and appears to be set mainly in childhood and adolescence. Within that stable population there's steady turnover: about **10% of fat cells are replaced each year**, at every adult age and body size. Old cells die, new ones are born, and the total holds steady.

So weight loss shrinks fat cells rather than deleting them. That's one small piece of why maintaining weight loss can be hard: the storage capacity is still there, waiting to be refilled. It's not a reason for discouragement. It's a reason to treat maintenance as its own skill, rather than assuming the job ends when the scale hits a number.
What the scale is really telling you

Once you think about weight as atoms coming and going, the daily bathroom scale makes a lot more sense, and becomes a lot less emotional. Your body weight at any moment includes the food still moving through your gut, the water in your tissues, and the stored carbohydrate in your muscles and liver, which holds onto water as well. All of those can swing noticeably from one day to the next, while the slow process of fat loss is trickling out underneath.

A salty galley meal, a hard workout, a long watch without much water, or a few extra hours of sleep can all move the number without changing your fat at all. That's why single readings are close to useless and trends over weeks are what matter. The fat leaving your body never shows up as a dramatic drop on any one morning. It leaves in small amounts with every breath, and you only see it when you zoom out.

The same logic exposes a classic gym myth. Sweating hard in a hot room or a heavy jacket can make the scale drop quickly, but what you lost is water, and it comes right back when you drink. Sweat is your body cooling itself, not fat melting. The fat-burning part of a workout is the extra oxygen your muscles used and the extra CO2 you breathed out, which is much quieter and much slower.
So should you just breathe harder?

If fat leaves through your lungs, the obvious joke is to breathe faster. It doesn't work. Breathing doesn't drive fat loss; metabolism does. Your breathing rate simply follows how much CO2 your cells are producing. Breathing more than your metabolism needs, which is hyperventilation, doesn't burn anything extra and can make you dizzy, give you palpitations, or even cause you to pass out.

What does raise the output is using more energy. Meerman and Brown estimated that a person at rest exhales at least around 200 grams of carbon a day. Replacing one hour of rest with moderate exercise like jogging removes roughly **40 grams** more carbon, about a 20% increase for that day. That's real, and it adds up. But they also pointed out how easily food puts it back: a 100-gram muffin supplies about a fifth of a typical person's daily energy needs.

This is the clearest way to see weight loss in physical terms. Carbon atoms come in through food and drink. Carbon atoms go out mostly through your breath. If, over time, more carbon leaves than arrives, the difference has to come from storage, and your fat stores shrink. Every diet that works, whatever its branding, works by tilting that carbon balance.

blocks.title: Common answers vs what actually happens

left.head: What most people say
items: Fat is converted into energy or heat
Fat leaves as waste in the toilet
Fat turns into muscle
Ab exercises burn belly fat

right.head: What the chemistry says
items: Energy is released, but the atoms remain and must exit
About 84% of the mass leaves as exhaled CO2
Fat and muscle are different tissues; one can't become the other
Fat is drawn from all over the body through the blood

blocks.text: Where your fat goes next

There's a last twist that makes this more than a biology trivia answer. The carbon you exhale doesn't stay gone. It joins the air, where plants and algae take it in through photosynthesis and build it into sugars, starches and oils. Animals eat the plants. People eat both. Some of that carbon eventually ends up stored as fat in somebody, and the loop continues.

blocks.title: The carbon loop running through you
items: Plants capture CO2 from the air
Carbon becomes food: grains, fruit, oils, animals
You eat it, and surplus carbon is stored as fat
Your cells oxidize the fat for energy
You exhale the carbon as CO2

blocks.text: On a submarine, the loop takes a detour. The air is a closed system, so the CO2 the crew breathes out has to be removed by the boat's atmosphere control equipment, or it would build up to dangerous levels. Every crew member who leans out over a long deployment is, quite literally, sending their former fat into the scrubbers.

The idea worth keeping isn't just the trivia. It's how easy it is to accept a vague answer that sounds right, like fat burns off, without asking where the atoms go. Meerman's question was simple enough for a child to ask, yet most experts had never thought it through. Asking where things physically go is a habit that pays off far beyond nutrition. And next time progress feels invisible, remember that it literally is: the fat you lose leaves quietly, one breath at a time, all day and all night.

takeaways: About 84% of lost fat leaves as exhaled CO2; the other 16% leaves as water.
Losing 10 kg of fat takes 29 kg of inhaled oxygen and produces 28 kg of CO2 and 11 kg of water.
Fat is drawn from all over the body, so you can't spot-reduce with targeted exercises.
Fat cells shrink when you lose fat, but their number stays roughly constant in adults.
Breathing harder doesn't help; using more energy than you eat over time is what tilts the carbon balance.

title: The Slowest Emergency: Why We Age, and Whether We Have To
dek: Your risk of dying roughly doubles every decade of adult life. Biologists now argue about whether that curve is fate, or a treatable condition.

blocks.text: Here is aging, expressed as a single number. According to the Social Security Administration's life tables, a 20-year-old American man has about a **1 in 770** chance of dying in the next twelve months. At 50, it's about 1 in 176. At 80, about 1 in 16. At 90, about 1 in 6.

Nothing dramatic happens on any particular birthday. There's no switch. But the odds keep climbing, year after year, at a pace that accelerates. In 1825 a British actuary named Benjamin Gompertz noticed this pattern in mortality records and described it with a simple exponential curve. Two centuries later, his law still describes human populations remarkably well.

blocks.title: Chance of dying within a year, US men
blocks.source: US Social Security Administration, Period Life Table 2022 (2025 Trustees Report)

blocks.text: From 50 onward in that table, the annual risk roughly doubles or more every ten years. That curve is what aging *is*, from a statistician's point of view: not wrinkles or gray hair, but a steadily rising chance that something will go fatally wrong. The interesting questions are why the curve exists at all, and whether it has to bend upward the way it does.
Not a law of physics

You might assume that wearing out is simply what happens to complex machines, like a car accumulating rust. But aging isn't universal in the way physics is. The clearest counterexample is a small, wrinkled, nearly hairless animal from East Africa: the naked mole-rat.

Naked mole-rats are about the size of a mouse, yet they've been recorded living more than 30 years, where a lab mouse is old at two or three. In 2018, researchers analyzed more than 3,000 lifespan records and found something no one had documented in a mammal before. Their risk of death *didn't increase with age*, even at ages far beyond when they become able to breed. By Gompertz's standard, they barely age at all.

Some other species, including certain turtles, fish and the tiny freshwater animal hydra, also appear to show little or no rise in mortality with age. That doesn't make them immortal; they still die from predators, disease and accidents. But it proves that rising mortality isn't an unavoidable property of being alive. It's a trait, and traits have evolutionary explanations.
Why evolution lets us fall apart

The explanation that most biologists accept was developed in the mid-twentieth century by Peter Medawar, George Williams and later Tom Kirkwood. It starts with a simple observation: in the wild, most animals die young from external causes like predators, starvation, cold and disease, long before they could die of old age.

That means natural selection gets weaker with age. A gene that causes trouble at age 80 barely matters to evolution if almost nobody in the ancestral environment survived to 80, because by then they'd already have had their children. Harmful late-acting effects slip through the filter, generation after generation.

It gets worse. Some genes may be actively favored because they help early in life, even if they cause damage later. Williams called this *antagonistic pleiotropy*: one gene, two effects, pointing in opposite directions over a lifetime. Something that boosts growth and fertility at 20 can be selected for even if it raises cancer risk at 70.

Kirkwood added an economic version, the *disposable soma* theory. Every organism has a limited energy budget. Energy spent maintaining and repairing the body is energy not spent on growing and reproducing. Evolution tunes the budget for a body that's expected to last about as long as it's likely to survive in the wild, not a day longer. Repair is good enough, never perfect, and the small errors pile up.

From evolution's point of view, your body was never designed to last forever. It was designed to stay in good enough condition long enough to pass on your genes. Everything after that is running on leftover engineering.
What actually goes wrong

If aging is the slow accumulation of unrepaired damage, what kinds of damage are we talking about? In 2013, a team led by Carlos López-Otín in Spain proposed a list of hallmarks of aging in the journal *Cell*. It became one of the most cited papers in the field. In 2023 they updated it to twelve hallmarks.
To count as a hallmark, a process had to meet three tests: it shows up with age, making it worse in experiments speeds up aging, and fixing it slows aging down. The current list:

items: **Genomic instability:** DNA damage accumulates faster than it's fully repaired.
**Telomere attrition:** the protective caps on chromosomes shorten with cell divisions.
**Epigenetic alterations:** the chemical tags that control which genes are on or off drift out of order.
**Loss of proteostasis:** cells get worse at folding proteins correctly and clearing out the bad ones.
**Disabled autophagy:** the cell's internal recycling system slows down.
**Deregulated nutrient sensing:** growth and fuel-sensing pathways like mTOR and insulin signaling get miscalibrated.
**Mitochondrial dysfunction:** the cell's power plants become less efficient.
**Cellular senescence:** damaged cells stop dividing but don't die, and send out inflammatory signals.
**Stem cell exhaustion:** the reserves that replenish tissues run low.
**Altered intercellular communication:** signals between cells and tissues get noisy.
**Chronic inflammation:** a low-grade, constant immune activation sometimes called inflammaging.
**Dysbiosis:** the gut's microbial community shifts in unhealthy ways.

blocks.text: Notice that several of these are things the body normally handles well. Cells repair DNA constantly, recycle damaged parts, and clear out broken proteins. Aging isn't the sudden appearance of new problems so much as the slow erosion of maintenance systems that once kept up with routine wear.

Anyone who has worked on a ship will recognize the pattern. A well-run boat can stay in service for decades, not because nothing breaks, but because a maintenance system catches small failures before they spread. Let that system slip, even a little, and deferred repairs start compounding: one degraded component strains the next. Aging looks a lot like a body whose maintenance schedule is slowly falling behind.

These aren't independent problems. Damaged DNA can push a cell into senescence. Senescent cells drive inflammation. Inflammation impairs stem cells. The hallmarks feed each other, which helps explain why aging accelerates instead of creeping along at a constant pace. It's less like a single part rusting and more like an organization where small failures in one department start overloading the others.

Some of these were spotted early. In 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead showed that normal human cells grown in a dish can only divide a limited number of times before they stop. That limit, now called the Hayflick limit, was later linked to telomeres, and it overturned the belief that cells could divide forever if kept in the right conditions.
Slowing the clock, in animals
If the hallmarks are real causes, then targeting them should slow aging. In animals, that has now been shown several times, and the results are among the most striking in modern biology.

blocks.title: Milestones in the science of aging
items: Gompertz describes the exponential rise of death risk with age
Hayflick and Moorhead show normal human cells have a division limit
Rapamycin extends lifespan in mice even when started late in life
The original hallmarks of aging are published in Cell
Clearing senescent cells extends healthy lifespan in mice
Naked mole-rats shown to defy Gompertz's law
The hallmarks list is updated to twelve

blocks.text: In 2009, a US program that tests possible anti-aging compounds in genetically diverse mice reported that **rapamycin**, a drug that dampens the mTOR nutrient-sensing pathway, extended lifespan in both sexes. Remarkably, the mice didn't start the drug until they were 600 days old, well into middle age. The effect was replicated at three separate test sites.

In 2016, a team at the Mayo Clinic used genetically engineered mice whose senescent cells could be destroyed on command with a drug. Starting at one year of age, clearing those cells extended median lifespan and delayed age-related decline in the kidneys, heart and fat tissue, with no obvious side effects.

items.label: Lifespan gain in female / male mice given rapamycin from 600 days (age at 90% mortality)
Median lifespan gain in mice after clearing senescent cells

blocks.source: Harrison et al., Nature, 2009; Baker et al., Nature, 2016

blocks.text: Calorie restriction, eating well below normal intake without malnutrition, extends lifespan in many species. In monkeys, two long-running US studies started in the 1980s seemed to disagree: one found a survival benefit, the other didn't. A joint analysis in 2017 concluded that differences in study design explained much of the gap, and that the health benefits held up in both.

Now the caveats, which matter a lot. Mice aren't people. Rapamycin suppresses parts of the immune system and has real side effects. Strict calorie restriction is hard to sustain and risky for many people, particularly anyone young, training hard or with a history of disordered eating. None of this is a reason to self-experiment with drugs or extreme diets. Ask a doctor before trying anything marketed as anti-aging, and be especially skeptical of supplements with mouse data and a sales page.
Is aging a disease?

Here's where biology turns into philosophy. Aging is the biggest risk factor for almost every major killer in wealthy countries: heart disease, most cancers, stroke, dementia. Medicine attacks these one at a time. But if you cure one disease in an 85-year-old, the rising tide of aging tends to deliver another one soon after. Some researchers argue that this one-at-a-time approach has diminishing returns, and that we should target the underlying process instead.

That idea, often called *geroscience*, comes with a provocative claim: aging should be treated as a medical condition, something we could prevent or slow. Supporters point out that our current system only approves drugs for specific diseases, so a drug that delayed many diseases at once would have no obvious regulatory path. Trials like the proposed TAME study of metformin have been designed partly to test whether regulators would accept a combined set of age-related diseases as an outcome.

Critics push back from several directions. If something happens to every human who lives long enough, calling it a disease stretches the word until it means nothing. Labeling old age itself as pathology risks fueling ageism, or encouraging doctors to shrug off treatable problems as just aging. And some demographers argue there are hard limits. A 2016 analysis in *Nature* found that survival gains slow sharply after age 100, and that the maximum age at death had stopped rising since the 1990s. The oldest documented person, Jeanne Calment, died in 1997 at 122. Other researchers disputed that analysis, and the debate continues.

blocks.title: Should aging be treated as a condition?

left.head: The case for
items: Aging drives most major chronic diseases
Treating diseases one at a time has diminishing returns
Animal studies show aging can be slowed
A medical label could unlock research and approval

right.head: The case against
items: Something universal isn't a disease in the normal sense
Risk of ageism and dismissing treatable illness
Human evidence for anti-aging drugs is still thin
There may be hard limits to human lifespan

blocks.text: What this means at twenty

Aging feels irrelevant at twenty, but the biology says otherwise. The hallmarks don't switch on at 60. They accumulate from early adulthood, quietly, at a rate that's partly set by genes and partly by how you live. The tools with the strongest evidence for a longer healthy life in humans are unglamorous: regular exercise, keeping muscle, not smoking, sleeping enough, staying socially connected, and avoiding the slow damage of excess. None of them come in a bottle.

It also helps to separate two ideas that get blurred together: *lifespan*, how long you live, and *healthspan*, how long you live in good health. Many geroscientists say the second is the real goal. Stretching out the frail final years isn't the prize. Compressing them, so that people stay strong and sharp until close to the end, is. The mouse studies are exciting partly because the treated animals didn't just live longer; several of their organs aged more slowly too.

Researchers are also building ways to measure aging directly, rather than waiting decades to count deaths. One approach, the so-called *epigenetic clock*, estimates biological age from the pattern of chemical tags on DNA, one of the twelve hallmarks. These clocks are still being refined, and commercial tests that promise to reveal your true age deserve skepticism. But the idea behind them is powerful: two people born the same year can be aging at visibly different speeds.

The deeper reframe is this. We usually think of age as a date on an ID card. Biologists increasingly think of it as a *rate*: how fast damage builds up relative to how well it's repaired. You can't change your birth year. But the steepness of the curve, at least some of it, is still being decided, and much of the deciding happens decades before anyone thinks to worry about it.

takeaways: Aging, statistically, is a death risk that roughly doubles each decade of adult life.
Evolution lets us age because natural selection weakens after reproductive years.
Biologists list twelve interconnected hallmarks of aging, from DNA damage to chronic inflammation.
Rapamycin and clearing senescent cells extend lifespan in mice, but human evidence is thin. Don't self-experiment.
The best-supported tools for healthy aging are boring ones: exercise, muscle, sleep, not smoking.
