title: The Autocomplete That Learned Too Much
dek: Every chatbot answer is built one word-fragment at a time by a machine trained only to guess what comes next. The real question is what it had to learn to guess well.

blocks.text: Type a question into a chatbot and watch the answer come back. It doesn't arrive all at once. It streams in a few characters at a time, like someone typing on the other end. That stutter isn't a design flourish. It's a window into the machine: the model is literally producing its answer one small piece at a time, and every piece is a guess.

When OpenAI introduced GPT-2 in 2019, it boiled the whole training goal down to one line. The model was trained to “predict the next word, given all of the previous words.” That's it. No grammar rules, no built-in encyclopedia, no logic module. Everything a modern **large language model** (LLM) does, from writing code to explaining reactor physics, grows out of that one almost insultingly simple objective, repeated at enormous scale.
Which raises the real puzzle: how does next-word guessing turn into something that can debug your script or walk you through a circuit? To see it, you have to follow a sentence through the machine.
Step one: turning words into numbers

A neural network can only do arithmetic, so text has to become numbers first. The model's first move is to chop your input into **tokens**, chunks of text from a fixed vocabulary. A common word like “the” is usually a single token. A rarer word gets split into fragments, so “unbelievably” might become “un,” “believ” and “ably.” This is why models sometimes fumble at counting the letters in a word: they never see letters, only chunks.

Each token is then swapped for a long list of numbers called an **embedding**. Think of it as coordinates in a space with thousands of dimensions. In GPT-3, every token became a list of 12,288 numbers. Nobody hand-assigns those coordinates. They are learned during training, and they end up arranged so that tokens used in similar ways sit near each other. “Reactor” lands closer to “turbine” than to “sandwich,” not because anyone said so, but because of the company those words keep in billions of sentences.
Step two: attention, the trick that changed everything

For years, language models read text like a ticker tape: one word at a time, left to right, carrying a fading memory of what came before. Long sentences broke them. In 2017 a team at Google published a paper with a cocky title, “Attention Is All You Need,” introducing the **transformer**. Its central idea was to let every token look directly at every other token in the passage and decide which ones matter to it.

Mechanically, it works like this. For each token, the model computes three vectors: a **query** (what am I looking for?), a **key** (what do I offer?) and a **value** (what information do I pass along if chosen?). Each token compares its query against every other token's key. Strong matches get high scores, the scores are squashed into weights that add up to one, and the token absorbs a weighted blend of everyone's values. After one round of attention, each token's numbers carry a bit of context from the whole passage.

Take the sentence “The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.” What does “it” mean? You know instantly: the trophy. In a transformer, the token “it” sends out its query, and a trained model weights “trophy” heavily, because big things not fitting into containers is how trophies and suitcases work. Change “big” to “small” and the right answer flips to the suitcase. Attention is the machinery that lets the model make that call.

blocks.title: What happens to your prompt
items: Your text is split into tokens, chunks from a fixed vocabulary
Each token becomes an embedding: a long list of learned numbers
Attention lets every token pull in context from every other token
Feed-forward layers transform each token's updated numbers
This repeats through dozens of stacked layers (96 in GPT-3)
The last layer gives a probability for every possible next token
One token is picked and appended, and the whole stack runs again

blocks.text: A transformer stacks this many times over. GPT-3 had 96 layers, each with 96 attention “heads” running side by side, so different heads can specialize: one tracking which noun a pronoun points to, another tracking open quote marks or unclosed brackets in code. The design also suited the hardware. Because all the tokens are processed at once instead of in sequence, transformers run well on GPUs, chips built to do thousands of multiplications in parallel. The original paper's base model trained in about 12 hours on eight GPUs. That efficiency is what made the next decade of scaling possible.

At the top of the stack, the model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, converted into probabilities. After “The capital of France is,” almost all the probability piles onto “Paris.” The system then **samples** one token, appends it to the text, and runs the entire stack again to get the next one. A setting called **temperature** controls how adventurous that pick is: low temperature nearly always takes the top choice, high temperature gives long shots a chance. Every chatbot answer you have ever read was assembled this way, one draw at a time.

There's also a hard limit on how much the model can see at once, called the **context window**. GPT-3's was 2,048 tokens, roughly a few pages of text. Anything outside the window simply doesn't exist for the model; it has no memory between conversations unless the text is fed back in. When a long chat starts “forgetting” what you said at the beginning, that's usually the window, not a lapse in attention. Newer models have far larger windows, but the principle is the same: the model only knows what's in front of it plus what's baked into its parameters.
Step three: how 175 billion knobs get set

All of that machinery is defined by **parameters**, the numbers inside the model that decide how embeddings are formed, how queries and keys are computed, and how each layer transforms its input. Before training they are random, and the model outputs gibberish. Training is the process of nudging them, and the loop is brutally simple.

blocks.title: The training loop
items: Show a passage with the next token hidden
The model predicts probabilities for every token
Measure how wrong it was about the real next token
Backpropagation traces the error back to every parameter
Nudge every parameter slightly to shrink the error

blocks.text: The tracing step, **backpropagation**, is just the chain rule from calculus applied very carefully: it works out, for each of billions of parameters, which direction to move it so the right answer would have been a little more likely. Move them all a tiny bit, then repeat with the next chunk of text, trillions of times. This is **gradient descent**: walking downhill on a landscape of error, one small step at a time, without ever seeing the whole map.

Then comes scale. GPT-2 had 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3, a year later, had 175 billion and was trained on 300 billion tokens, mostly filtered web pages plus books and Wikipedia. The industry assumption was that bigger was the main lever. In 2022, DeepMind ran a large set of training experiments and concluded the field had been following the wrong recipe.

blocks.title: Model size, billions of parameters
blocks.note: Chinchilla was a quarter of Gopher's size and beat it across a wide range of tests.
blocks.source: OpenAI, 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022

blocks.text: Their finding: for a fixed computing budget, model size and training data should grow together. Double the parameters, double the tokens. By that rule, giant models like DeepMind's own 280-billion-parameter Gopher were badly undertrained, all brain and not enough reading. To prove it, they trained Chinchilla, a quarter of Gopher's size, on 1.4 trillion tokens, about 20 tokens per parameter, using the same compute. It outperformed Gopher and GPT-3 across a large range of tasks.

blocks.title: Training data, billions of tokens
blocks.note: Llama 3's figure is reported as “over 15 trillion” tokens.
blocks.source: Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Hugging Face, 2024

blocks.text: The industry took the lesson and then sprinted past it. Meta's Llama 3 models, released in 2024 at 8 and 70 billion parameters, were trained on more than 15 trillion tokens. For the 8-billion model, that's nearly 2,000 tokens per parameter, nearly a hundred times Chinchilla's ratio. The logic is economic: a model is trained once but run for millions of users, so a smaller model that has read far more is cheaper every time anyone asks it something.
From autocomplete to assistant

A model trained only on next-token prediction, called a **base model**, isn't an assistant. It's a document continuer. Ask it “How do I troubleshoot a ground fault?” and it might reply with three more questions, because on the internet, questions often show up in lists of questions. It has learned the shape of text, not the job of answering.

Turning it into an assistant takes a second phase. First, people write example conversations showing good answers, and the model is fine-tuned on them. Then comes **reinforcement learning from human feedback** (RLHF): the model writes several answers, humans rank them, a separate model learns to predict those rankings, and the language model is tuned to produce answers that score well. In OpenAI's 2022 InstructGPT study, raters preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained this way over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. A model more than 100 times smaller won, because it had been taught what the job was.

blocks.title: Base model vs. tuned assistant

left.head: Base model
items: Trained only to continue text
Treats your question as the start of a document
Imitates whatever it's shown, good or bad
Knows a lot, but not what you want

right.head: Tuned assistant
items: Further trained on example conversations
Treats your message as a request to answer
Shaped by human rankings of better and worse answers
Same knowledge, aimed at being useful

blocks.text: Why it makes things up

The flaw everyone has met is **hallucination**: a fluent, confident, completely wrong answer. A citation to a paper that doesn't exist. A function that isn't in the library. Once you understand the training objective, this stops being mysterious. The model was never trained to say true things. It was trained to say likely things, and most of the time likely and true overlap. When they don't, nothing inside the model raises a flag.

A 2025 paper by Adam Kalai and colleagues at OpenAI and Georgia Tech sharpened this into two arguments. First, some facts are essentially arbitrary, like a particular person's birthday. If a fact shows up only once in the training data, there's no pattern to learn from, and the authors argue the error rate on that kind of fact should be at least as high as the share of such facts that appear just once. Second, the grading makes it worse. Most benchmarks award a point for a right answer and nothing for “I don't know,” so a model that always guesses scores at least as well as one that honestly admits uncertainty.

If you've ever bluffed a multiple-choice question, you've done what the model does. When a blank scores zero, guessing is the rational move. Treat a chatbot's confidence as a writing style, not as evidence.

The practical upshot: LLMs are strongest where you can check the output. Code runs or it doesn't. A math step can be verified. A summary can be compared against the document in front of you. They are weakest on obscure specifics, such as exact figures, names, citations and niche regulations, which are precisely the things that appear rarely in training data. Use one like a sharp shipmate who has read everything once and never admits when he's fuzzy: great for ideas, explanations and first drafts, never the final word on a value that matters.
Is it “just” autocomplete?

Critics like to say an LLM is “just predicting the next word,” as if that settled things. It doesn't, because it hides how hard the prediction can get. To predict the next line of a physics derivation, it helps to model the physics. To predict how a character in a novel responds, it helps to model what she wants. Nobody programmed those abilities in. Training simply rewards whatever internal machinery lowers prediction error, and over trillions of tokens, some fairly sophisticated machinery pays for itself.

Researchers have started looking at that machinery directly. In 2024, Anthropic reported extracting millions of internal **features** from one of its Claude models: recurring patterns of neuron activity that line up with human concepts. One responded to the Golden Gate Bridge whether it was named in English, mentioned in other languages or shown in a picture. When researchers artificially turned that feature up, the model began insisting it was the bridge. That isn't proof of understanding in the human sense, and whether these systems “know” anything is a genuinely open argument. But it shows the inside isn't a lookup table of stored phrases. It's a learned map of concepts, and parts of that map can be read.

Here's the reframe worth keeping. Nuke school drills into you the difference between someone who can recite a procedure and someone who understands the plant well enough to predict what happens next. A language model sits in a strange spot on that spectrum. It was only ever graded on prediction, and prediction at this scale pushed it to build something like understanding along the way: patchy, alien and sometimes confidently wrong. So the interesting question isn't whether it's “just” predicting. It's how much of what we call understanding is, underneath, very good prediction.

takeaways: An LLM writes one token at a time; every token is a weighted guess about what comes next.
Attention lets every word look at every other word, which is how a model resolves context like what “it” refers to.
Since Chinchilla, data matters as much as size: today's models read trillions of tokens.
Hallucinations follow from the objective. The model learned what's likely, not what's true, so verify specifics.
“Just predicting the next word” undersells it: predicting well forces a model to learn a lot about the world.

title: The Internet Is a Garden Hose on the Seafloor
dek: Your messages get shredded into pieces, fired across a network that promises nothing, and rebuilt on the other side of an ocean in a blink. Here's how that actually works.

blocks.text: At 10:30 on the night of October 29, 1969, a UCLA student programmer named Charley Kline sat at a terminal and tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, hundreds of miles up the coast. He typed an L. It arrived. He typed an O. It arrived. He typed a G, and the system on the other end crashed.

So the first message ever sent over the network that became the internet was “lo.” About an hour later they got the full login working, and the rest is history: a network that started with a crash now carries video calls, bank transfers, game matches and nearly everything else. Yet most people who use it every waking hour couldn't tell you what happens between pressing send and the message showing up. The answer involves a radical design idea, a pair of protocols, and a lot of glass lying on the bottom of the ocean.
Chop it up: the packet idea

The old telephone network worked by **circuit switching**. When you made a call, the system reserved a continuous path of wire for you, end to end, for as long as you talked. That's simple and reliable, but wasteful: the line sits reserved even during silences, and if any link on the path fails, the call dies.

The internet does something stranger. It chops every message into small chunks called **packets**, each with a header stating where it's going and where it came from, like a label on a parcel. Packets are launched into the network independently. Each one may take a different route, and they can arrive out of order. Nobody reserves anything. The wire carries your packets, then someone else's, then yours again, interleaved with millions of other conversations.

It's the difference between booking a private train for one passenger and putting everyone in shared traffic. Shared traffic is messier, but it uses the roads far more efficiently, and when one road is closed, cars just go around. That resilience was the point: a network with no central switchboard has no single place where cutting a wire kills everything.
Two protocols, one division of labor

In May 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published a paper describing a way to link separate packet networks into one, an *inter-net*. Their design eventually split into two layers that still run your phone today, and the split is the most important idea in this article.

The bottom layer is **IP**, the Internet Protocol. Its job is addressing and forwarding, and nothing else. Every device gets an IP address, and every **router** (the specialized computers at network junctions) looks at a packet's destination address, consults a table, and passes it one hop closer. That's it. IP makes no promises. Packets can be dropped when a router is overloaded, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order. Engineers call this **best effort**, which is a polite way of saying no guarantees.

How does a router know which way to send things? Each network on the internet, whether a phone carrier, a university or a cloud company, announces to its neighbors which blocks of addresses it can reach, using a protocol called **BGP** (Border Gateway Protocol). Those announcements ripple outward until every major router holds a rough map: for addresses in this range, hand the packet to that neighbor. No router knows the full path. Each knows only the next hop, like a messenger relaying a note down a passageway who only needs to know who's next in line.

BGP runs largely on trust, and that's its weak spot. If a network mistakenly announces that it can reach addresses it can't, traffic can be pulled toward it and vanish, and serious outages have started exactly that way. Internet routing is less a single designed machine than a constantly renegotiated agreement among a huge number of independent operators, none of whom is in charge.

The layer on top is **TCP**, the Transmission Control Protocol, and it turns that chaos into a reliable stream. Before sending data, two machines perform a **three-way handshake**: one says “let's talk” (SYN), the other says “got it, let's talk” (SYN-ACK), and the first confirms (ACK). Then every byte gets a sequence number. The receiver sends back acknowledgments of what arrived. Anything not acknowledged in time gets sent again. Out-of-order packets are put back in order before your app ever sees them. TCP also watches for signs of congestion, such as lost packets, and slows down when the network is clogged, so millions of users don't jointly stampede it into collapse.

blocks.title: Who does what

left.head: IP (the network)
items: Gives every device an address
Routers forward packets one hop at a time
No guarantee of delivery or order
Simple, fast, and dumb on purpose

right.head: TCP (the endpoints)
items: Handshake sets up a connection
Numbers every byte and confirms receipt
Resends whatever goes missing
Slows down when the network is congested

blocks.text: Notice where the intelligence lives. The network in the middle is kept dumb, and the reliability is built by the two computers at the ends. That's deliberate. A dumb core is cheap to build and easy to extend, and it doesn't need to understand what you're doing. It didn't need upgrading when video streaming or online gaming arrived. New ideas could be invented at the edges without asking permission from anyone in the middle.

Fast-paced online games often show the trade-off from the other side. Many skip TCP's guarantees for some traffic and use a lighter protocol called **UDP**, which just fires packets without handshakes or resends. If a position update from half a second ago went missing, resending it is pointless; the game wants the newest data, not a perfect history. When you see an enemy teleport, you're watching that design choice play out.

blocks.title: What happens when you hit send
items: Your app hands the message to TCP, which splits it into numbered segments
IP wraps each one in a packet stamped with source and destination addresses
Your router passes packets to your provider's network, then onto the backbone
Routers forward each packet hop by hop, possibly along different paths
Packets cross oceans as pulses of light in undersea fiber
The receiving TCP acknowledges, reorders, and requests anything missing
The rebuilt message is handed to the app on the other end

blocks.text: One step quietly happens before all of that: names. Computers route by number, but you type names. So your device first asks the **Domain Name System** (DNS), a distributed and hierarchical phone book, to translate a name like a website address into an IP address. Answers get cached at several levels, close to you, so popular lookups rarely have to travel far. When DNS breaks, the network can be perfectly healthy and yet nothing seems to load, which is why it gets blamed for so many mysterious outages.

The design spread slowly, then all at once. On January 1, 1983, DARPA required the ARPANET to switch from its older protocol to TCP/IP, a cutover remembered as a kind of flag day for the modern internet. The addressing scheme, though, was sized for a research network. The original version, IPv4, has 2 to the 32nd power addresses, a little over four billion. On February 3, 2011, the central pool of unassigned IPv4 blocks ran dry when the last ones were handed out to the regional registries.

blocks.title: From “lo” to now
items: First ARPANET message: “lo,” then a crash
Cerf and Kahn publish the design for TCP
ARPANET switches over to TCP/IP on January 1
The central pool of IPv4 addresses runs out
IPv6 passes 50% of users reaching Google

blocks.text: The fix is **IPv6**, with 2 to the 128th power addresses, roughly 340 trillion trillion trillion. Adoption crawled for years because IPv4 kept limping along with workarounds. Then, on March 28, 2026, Google's measurements showed IPv6 access to its services topping 50% of users for the first time. A transition decades in the making finally crossed the halfway mark.
The cloud is underwater

People talk about “the cloud” as if data floats through the sky. When your packets leave the continent, they almost certainly travel through glass on the seafloor. TeleGeography, the research firm that maps these systems, tracks more than 600 active and planned submarine cables and estimates over 1.5 million kilometers of them in service, enough to wrap around the planet dozens of times. Satellites carry only a sliver of international traffic. Using older FCC data, the firm notes satellites accounted for just 0.37% of U.S. international capacity.

items.label: Submarine cable in service worldwide (early 2026)
Cable faults per year
Share of faults caused by fishing gear and ship anchors

blocks.source: TeleGeography Submarine Cable FAQ, 2026 (citing the International Cable Protection Committee)

blocks.text: For most of their length, these cables are about as thick as a garden hose. Inside, the actual data rides in glass fibers about the width of a human hair, surrounded by layers of protection, with heavier armor near shore where the dangers are. Light pulses go in one end, are boosted by amplifiers spaced along the route, and come out the other. A single modern cable can carry staggering volumes; the MAREA cable across the Atlantic is rated at a potential 224 terabits per second.

They also break, a lot. The International Cable Protection Committee counts roughly 200 faults a year, and about two-thirds come from fishing gear and dragged anchors, not sabotage or sharks. Fish bites, a favorite internet myth, caused zero recorded faults between 2007 and 2014. When a cable goes down, traffic reroutes across other cables while a repair ship grapples the broken ends up from the bottom. That's the packet idea scaled to a planet: no single path is sacred.

Ownership has shifted too. Cables used to be built by consortiums of phone companies. Now the big buyers are content companies such as Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon, which lay their own routes to link their data centers. The physical internet is increasingly private infrastructure.
The speed limit you can't patch

Here's the part software can't fix. Light in glass travels slower than in a vacuum, roughly two-thirds as fast, around 204,000 kilometers per second. That works out to about 5 milliseconds of one-way delay for every 1,000 kilometers of fiber. Cross an ocean and back and you've spent tens of milliseconds before any computer does any work at all.

That limit is worth real money. In 2015, the Hibernia Express cable opened between New York and London advertising round trips under 58.95 milliseconds, explicitly aimed at financial traders. When a price difference between two exchanges lasts only milliseconds, the firm on the shorter cable wins.

Most traffic gets nowhere near the physical limit. A 2018 study of internet fiber infrastructure found that measured latencies typically run about three times longer than a signal traveling in a straight line at light speed would need. Part of that is physics, since light in fiber is slower. The rest is routing: cables follow roads, railways and coastlines rather than straight lines, packets detour through distant exchange points, and routers add small delays at each hop.

blocks.title: How much slower the real internet is than its limits
blocks.note: Median values. “Fiber path vs straight” is how much longer cable routes are than line-of-sight distance.
blocks.source: Bozkurt et al., “Dissecting Latency in the Internet's Fiber Infrastructure,” 2018

blocks.text: Your ping to a server is mostly geography. Fiber routes, the number of hops and the distance to the data center set a floor that no gaming chair, router upgrade or faster plan can beat. Picking the closest server region usually matters more than anything else you control.
Reliable from unreliable

Step back and the whole system rests on a counterintuitive bet. Instead of building a network that never fails, the designers built one that fails constantly, in small ways, and made recovery automatic. Packets get dropped every second of every day. Cables get snagged by anchors a couple hundred times a year. Routers crash. And yet the message gets through, because no single part was ever trusted to be perfect.

That's an idea that reaches well beyond networking. Anyone who has stood watch in an engineering plant knows systems are designed around the assumption that components will fail: redundancy, independent checks, multiple paths to a safe state. TCP is the same philosophy in software. Expect loss, number everything, confirm receipt, retry, slow down when things get crowded.

It also says something about how to build anything that lasts, including habits and projects. The fragile approach demands every day go to plan, and collapses at the first dropped packet. The robust approach assumes some days will be lost, keeps track of what actually got done, and resends without drama. The internet doesn't work because nothing goes wrong. It works because something goes wrong all the time, and the system was built to shrug.

So the next time a message lands on the far side of the planet in a fraction of a second, picture what actually happened: your words were shredded into numbered fragments, flung into a network that promised nothing, pushed as flickers of light through a hose-thick cable lying in the dark on the ocean floor, and stitched back together by a protocol designed in the 1970s that still assumes the worst. It's a little miracle of pessimism.

takeaways: The internet splits every message into packets that travel independently and get reassembled at the destination.
IP just addresses and forwards; TCP adds reliability at the endpoints by numbering, confirming and resending.
Over 1.5 million km of undersea cable carry nearly all intercontinental traffic, and they break about 200 times a year.
Light in fiber sets a hard floor on latency: about 5 ms per 1,000 km one way, which is why server distance matters.
The core design lesson: build reliable systems from unreliable parts by expecting failure and recovering automatically.

title: Quantum Computers Aren't Faster Computers
dek: They don't try every answer at once. They do something stranger, it only pays off on a short list of problems, and one of those problems happens to be the lock on the internet.

blocks.text: In December 2024, Google announced a chip called Willow. It finished a benchmark calculation in under five minutes. Google estimated that one of the fastest classical supercomputers on Earth would need about 10 septillion years to do the same job. That's a 1 followed by 25 zeros, far longer than the universe has existed.

Read that and it's natural to imagine your next gaming PC running on qubits, loading instantly, rendering at a million frames per second. It won't. Willow can't run a web browser, and the problem it crushed was chosen because it is brutally hard for normal computers and almost useless for anything else.

So here's the puzzle: how can a machine be septillions of times faster than a supercomputer at one task and worse than your phone at almost everything else? The answer is the single most misunderstood idea in modern technology. A quantum computer isn't a faster computer. It's a different kind of instrument, and once you understand how it really works, you can tell the hype from the genuinely big deal.
The myth of trying every answer at once

Start with what a normal computer does. A *bit* is a switch that's either 0 or 1. Your CPU flips billions of them per second in a precise sequence. At every moment, the machine is in exactly one definite state, and you could, in principle, read out every bit without disturbing anything.

A *qubit* is different. Its state is described by two numbers called *amplitudes*, one attached to 0 and one attached to 1. Amplitudes behave a lot like waves: they have a size and a direction, so they can be positive, negative, or something in between. When you measure the qubit, you get a plain 0 or a plain 1, with odds set by the squared size of each amplitude. The measurement also destroys the delicate in-between state.

Now add more qubits. Two qubits need four amplitudes, one for each combination: 00, 01, 10, 11. Three need eight. Every added qubit doubles the count, so 300 qubits involve 2 to the 300th power amplitudes, a number vastly larger than the count of atoms in the observable universe. This is where the popular story comes from: a quantum computer explores all those possibilities in parallel, so it must be checking every answer at once.

Those combined amplitudes are also where *entanglement* comes from. When qubits are entangled, the amplitudes can't be split into separate descriptions for each qubit. The system only makes sense as a whole: measure one qubit and you instantly constrain what the others can show. Entanglement isn't a way to send messages faster than light, but it is the resource that lets a computation weave the possibilities of many qubits together instead of treating each one alone.

Here's the catch that the popular story leaves out. When you measure at the end, you get one answer, chosen at random according to the amplitudes. If all the possible answers have equal amplitudes, you just get a random guess. You could do that with a coin. All that enormous hidden state is worthless unless you can arrange for the wrong answers to fade and the right one to stand out before you look.

A quantum computer doesn't check every answer and report back. It sets up a pattern of waves so that wrong answers cancel each other out, then takes one measurement and hopes the right answer is the loudest thing left.
Interference is the real trick

If you've worked with AC power, you already have the intuition. Two signals in phase add up. Two signals 180 degrees out of phase cancel. Noise-cancelling headphones use the same idea, generating a wave that is the mirror image of the noise so that the two sum to nearly nothing.

Quantum algorithms are choreography for that kind of cancellation. Each step of the computation is a *gate*, an operation that rotates and mixes the amplitudes. A well-designed sequence of gates makes the paths leading to wrong answers arrive out of phase, so they cancel, while the paths leading to the right answer arrive in phase and reinforce. Then you measure, and with high probability you get the answer you wanted.

The hard part is that you can only build this choreography when the problem has some hidden structure the waves can lock onto, like a repeating pattern. Most everyday computing tasks have no such structure to exploit. That's why there is no quantum spreadsheet and probably never will be. The speedup is not a general property of the hardware. It belongs to specific algorithms for specific problems.

blocks.title: How a quantum algorithm actually runs
items: Prepare the qubits in a simple starting state, usually all zeros.
Apply gates that spread the amplitudes across many possible answers.
Apply more gates that encode the problem, shifting the phase of some paths.
Use interference so wrong answers cancel and the right one grows.
Measure once and read out a single classical answer.
Repeat several times and check the result on a normal computer.

blocks.text: The short list of things it's good at

The most famous example came in 1994, when Peter Shor, then at AT&T, showed that a quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently. Factoring means taking a number like 15 and finding the primes that multiply to make it, 3 and 5. For numbers hundreds of digits long, the best known classical methods take an impractically long time. Shor's algorithm turns factoring into a problem of finding the period of a repeating pattern, exactly the kind of structure that interference can latch onto.

In 1996, Lov Grover at Bell Labs found a broader but much smaller speedup. Imagine a phone directory of N names in random order, and you want the one with a given number. A classical search has to check about half the entries on average. Grover's algorithm needs only about the square root of N steps. For a million entries, that's on the order of a thousand steps instead of half a million. Useful, but it's a square-root gain, not the exponential leap Shor offers.

The third big category may matter most in the long run: simulating nature itself. Molecules and materials are quantum systems, and tracking their electrons on a classical computer gets exponentially harder as they grow. A quantum computer speaks the same language as the thing it's simulating. That's the hope behind designing better catalysts, batteries and drugs, and it's the area Google pointed to in October 2025 with an algorithm called Quantum Echoes, aimed at revealing hidden dynamics inside quantum systems like molecules.

blocks.title: Where quantum helps, and where it doesn't

left.head: Strong candidates
items: Factoring big numbers (Shor)
Simulating molecules and materials
Some search and optimization problems, with smaller gains
Sampling tasks designed to be hard classically

right.head: Poor fits
items: Gaming, video and graphics
Web browsing and everyday apps
Most business software and databases
Anything that needs to read out huge amounts of data

blocks.text: The noise problem

If quantum computing is so powerful for these problems, why haven't we broken anything yet? Because qubits are absurdly fragile. Any stray interaction with the outside world, whether heat, vibration or a passing electromagnetic field, leaks information out of the qubit and scrambles the amplitudes. Physicists call this *decoherence*. Superconducting chips like Google's are cooled to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero to slow it down, and even so, Willow's qubits hold their state for times approaching 100 microseconds.

Every gate also has a small chance of error. Google reported fidelities for Willow of 99.97 percent for single-qubit gates and 99.88 percent for the two-qubit gates that create entanglement. That sounds excellent until you remember that a useful algorithm needs millions or billions of operations, and errors stack up.

items.label: Physical qubits on Google's Willow chip
How long Willow's qubits hold their state
Fidelity of Willow's two-qubit gates

blocks.source: Google Quantum AI, Willow announcement (Dec 2024) and hardware update (Oct 2025)

blocks.text: The answer is *quantum error correction*. You spread one reliable *logical* qubit across many unreliable *physical* qubits and keep checking them for signs of damage, without directly measuring the information you're protecting. It's a bit like a RAID array or redundant instrument channels in a reactor plant: no single sensor is trusted, but the group can catch and correct a failure. The catch is that more qubits also means more places for errors to creep in. Error correction only wins if the hardware is already good enough. That cutoff is called the *threshold*.

There's a clever twist in how the checking works. You can't just look at the protected qubits, because measuring them would destroy the information. Instead, extra helper qubits are entangled with groups of data qubits and measured in their place. Their results reveal whether a neighbor has flipped, without revealing what the data actually is. A classical computer reads those results continuously and decides which corrections to apply, over and over in a continuous cycle for as long as the computation runs.

Willow's real headline wasn't the septillion years. It was that when Google grew its encoded qubit from a 3-by-3 grid of physical qubits to 5-by-5 and then 7-by-7, the error rate fell by half at each step. Bigger finally meant better. That's the first convincing sign that scaling up can work, though a useful machine needs vastly more qubits than 105.
A countdown on the internet's lock

Much of the internet's security has relied on public-key cryptography such as RSA, which depends on factoring being hopelessly slow. A big enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break it. So the question that matters is not whether a quantum computer is impressive. It's how big one would need to be.

In 2019, Craig Gidney and Martin Ekerå estimated that factoring a 2048-bit RSA key would take about 20 million noisy physical qubits running for eight hours. In May 2025, Gidney published a new estimate: fewer than a million noisy qubits, running for less than a week, assuming the same error rate of 0.1 percent per gate. The hardware didn't get 20 times better in six years. The *algorithms* did. That's a pattern worth remembering: in this field, the target moves from both ends.

blocks.title: Qubits needed to break RSA-2048 vs. qubits built
blocks.note: The 2025 figure is an upper bound ('less than a million'). Willow's bar is there; at 105 qubits it's too small to see.
blocks.source: Gidney & Ekerå, 2019; Gidney, arXiv 2505.15917, 2025; Google Quantum AI, 2024

blocks.text: Even so, the gap is enormous. Today's best chips have around a hundred physical qubits, and the requirement is still on the order of a million. Nobody can tell you with confidence when that gap closes. But there's a reason security agencies are moving now. Adversaries can record encrypted traffic today and simply store it, waiting for the day they can decrypt it. Security people call this *harvest now, decrypt later*. Secrets that need to stay secret for decades are already exposed to a future machine.

That's why, in August 2024, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized its first three post-quantum encryption standards, built on math problems that are believed to be hard for quantum computers too. One is meant for general encryption and two for digital signatures. NIST noted that some experts expect a code-breaking quantum computer within a decade. The software migration is starting long before the hardware exists, which is exactly how it should work.

blocks.title: From theory to countdown
items: Peter Shor shows a quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently
Lov Grover publishes a square-root speedup for unstructured search
Google's 53-qubit Sycamore claims a task in 200 seconds; IBM counters that a supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days
Aug 2024
NIST finalizes its first three post-quantum encryption standards
Dec 2024
Willow: 105 qubits, errors halve as the encoded qubit grows
May 2025
New estimate: RSA-2048 needs under a million noisy qubits
Oct 2025
Google reports verifiable quantum advantage with Quantum Echoes

blocks.text: How to read the next headline

The 2019 Sycamore claim is a useful lesson. Google said its 53-qubit chip did in 200 seconds what a supercomputer would need 10,000 years to do. IBM quickly argued that a smarter classical approach on the Summit supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days. Classical algorithms keep improving too, so every claim of quantum advantage is a race against a moving target. Some claims hold up, and some shrink.

It also helps to know what the famous benchmark actually is. *Random circuit sampling* means running a random jumble of gates and collecting the outputs. The results have no practical meaning. The point is that the pattern of outputs is extraordinarily hard to reproduce on a classical machine, which makes it a good stress test and a poor product. Google's October 2025 Quantum Echoes work was pitched as a step past this, because its result can be checked and is connected to real physics questions about molecules.

When you see the next big announcement, ask three questions. Is the task useful, or was it chosen because it's hard for classical machines? Can the answer be checked? And how many of the qubits are error-corrected logical qubits rather than raw physical ones? Those three questions cut through most of the noise.

The reframe to carry around is this. A quantum computer is to a normal computer what a telescope is to a truck. Nobody asks whether a telescope is faster than a truck. It does something a truck can't do at all, and it's useless for hauling groceries. The machines being built now are early, noisy telescopes. What they eventually reveal, whether it's new materials, new medicines or the contents of today's encrypted messages, depends on how fast the engineering closes a gap that is still measured in factors of ten thousand.

takeaways: Qubits hold many amplitudes, but a measurement gives one answer. The power comes from interference, not from checking every answer.
Big speedups exist only for problems with hidden structure: factoring, simulating molecules, and a few others.
Noise is the main obstacle; error correction spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones and only works below a quality threshold.
Breaking RSA-2048 was estimated at 20 million qubits in 2019 and under a million in 2025. Today's best chips have about a hundred.
Post-quantum encryption standards were finalized in 2024 because encrypted data can be stored now and decrypted later.

title: The Feed Knows What You'll Do, Not What You Want
dek: Recommendation algorithms are prediction machines aimed at your behavior. Once you see how they score you, the endless scroll stops looking like a window and starts looking like a mirror.

blocks.text: It's 0130 and you just got off watch. You tell yourself you'll check one thing before you rack out. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusted pocketknife, and you couldn't explain how you got there if someone paid you. You didn't really choose most of those videos. You just never said no to them.

That isn't a character flaw so much as an engineering result. In January 2018, YouTube's chief product officer, Neal Mohan, said that about 70 percent of the time people spend watching YouTube is driven by its recommendations. Netflix engineers wrote in 2015 that their recommender influenced roughly 80 percent of the hours streamed on the service. Most of what the world watches is no longer picked by the viewer. It's picked by a prediction.

To use these systems instead of being used by them, it helps to know what they actually are. They aren't mind readers, and they aren't villains. They are machines built to answer one narrow question, billions of times a day: *what will this person do next?*

items.label: Share of YouTube watch time driven by recommendations (2018)
Share of Netflix hours streamed influenced by its recommender (2015)
How long a typical Netflix member browses before losing interest

blocks.source: Neal Mohan at CES, reported by Quartz, 2018; Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems, 2015

blocks.text: A funnel, not a mind

Look at the problem from the platform's side. YouTube has an enormous library and a fraction of a second to fill your home screen. No model can carefully evaluate every video for every user in that time. So almost every large recommender is built as a funnel, with cheap, fast filtering at the top and slow, careful judgment at the bottom.

Google engineers described YouTube's version in a 2016 paper. The first stage, *candidate generation*, takes a corpus of millions of videos and pulls out a few hundred that are roughly relevant to you. It leans heavily on *collaborative filtering*: the idea that people who watched what you watched tend to want what those people watched next. The second stage, *ranking*, scores each of those few hundred carefully, using many more signals. A few dozen make it to your screen.

The trick that makes the first stage fast is called an *embedding*. Every video and every user gets turned into a list of numbers, a few hundred long, which you can picture as a point in a space with hundreds of dimensions. During training, the system nudges those points around so that the things you'd watch end up close to you. Finding candidates then becomes a geometry problem: grab the videos nearest your point.

Nobody writes down that one axis means tactical gear and another means sad piano covers. The model invents its own axes from billions of clicks, and many of them don't map onto any human category at all. That's part of why a feed can feel uncannily accurate and impossible to explain at the same time.

blocks.title: How a feed gets built in a fraction of a second
items: Start with the whole library: millions of items.
Candidate generation: cheaply pull a few hundred items that sit near your embedding.
Ranking: score each candidate with a bigger model and many more signals.
Filter and mix: drop repeats, spam and things you've seen; add some variety.
Show the top results and log everything you do with them.
Feed that log back into training, so tomorrow's model knows you a little differently.

blocks.text: What the machine is really predicting

Here is the part most people miss. The ranking model doesn't output a single verdict on how good a video is. It predicts a set of separate probabilities: the chance you'll click, watch to the end, like, reply, share, or tell it to go away. Then a plain formula combines those predictions into one score, and the highest scores win. The predictions are learned from data. The formula is chosen by people, and it encodes what the company has decided to value.

YouTube's 2016 paper is unusually frank about this. Its ranking objective was described as mostly a function of expected watch time per impression, rather than the chance of a click. The reason was practical: ranking by clicks tends to promote deceptive videos that people open and then abandon. Watch time was harder to fake. Notice what happened there. A human looked at a number, saw it being gamed, and swapped it for a different number.

We rarely get to see that formula. In 2023, Twitter (now X) published code for its home timeline ranker, including the weights it used as of April 2023. Each weight multiplies the predicted probability of one action. They're worth a close look, because they turn an abstract idea into a price list.

blocks.title: Twitter's ranking weights, April 2023 (like = 0.5)
blocks.note: Negative signals were weighted too: 'show less' or block at −74, a report at −369.
blocks.source: Twitter, the-algorithm-ml, home timeline ranker README, 2023

blocks.text: Read it like a menu. On that ranking, a predicted reply was worth 27 likes. A reply that the original poster then answered was worth 150 likes. A predicted report cost as much as 738 likes. Whoever set those numbers decided that conversation matters far more than quiet approval, and they were right that conversation keeps people on the app. What the formula didn't ask was whether the conversation was a friendly one or a shouting match.

Every platform makes a version of that choice. YouTube made a famous one in March 2012, when it told creators it would weight time watched more heavily than clicks when picking related and recommended videos. Clicks had been rewarding misleading thumbnails and titles. Watch time was supposed to reward videos people actually wanted to see.
Better serve videos that keep viewers entertained.

TikTok said in 2020 that one of its strongest signals is whether you finish a longer video from beginning to end, and that follower count is not a direct factor. Each of these is a sensible proxy for 'this person liked it.' None of them is the same thing as 'this person is glad they spent the time.'
The explore-exploit trap

A recommender faces a dilemma borrowed from casinos. Computer scientists call it the *multi-armed bandit* problem. A gambler facing a row of slot machines has to choose between pulling the one that has paid well so far (exploiting) and trying others that might pay better (exploring). Exploit too much and the feed goes stale. Explore too much and it fills with junk.

So feeds do both. Most of what you see is a confident bet, and a slice of it is a probe: something slightly outside your usual range, placed there to measure your reaction. That's why a strange video sometimes appears out of nowhere, and why one long look at it can tilt your feed for days. The system isn't messing with you. It's running an experiment, and you just answered it.

There's also a bias toward the past built into any model trained on yesterday's data. The YouTube engineers found that their system, left alone, underrated brand-new uploads, because popularity in the training data was averaged over the whole training window. Their fix was to tell the model how old each training example was, which raised watch time on fresh videos. Small design choices like that decide which creators get a shot and which never surface.

Put those pieces together and you get a loop, and loops are where the interesting behavior lives. Your actions train the model. The model decides what you see. What you see shapes your next actions. Anyone who has studied control systems knows that feedback can stabilize or it can drift. Watch three videos on a topic out of pure boredom, and the system may conclude that topic is who you are.

blocks.title: The feed loop
items: You act: watch, skip, like, linger
The model updates its picture of you
The feed shifts toward that picture
Your options narrow to what it shows
You act on those options

blocks.text: The same loop runs on the people making content. Anyone building a YouTube channel or a Roblox game is optimizing against a ranking formula whether they mean to or not. Strong hooks in the first seconds, faces in thumbnails, titles that open a question: creators drift toward these because the ranker rewards whatever predicts watching. The algorithm doesn't just learn its audience. It quietly trains everyone who makes things for it.
Wanting versus liking

If these models are so good at predicting behavior, why does an hour of scrolling so often feel like an hour you'd like back? Because behavior and satisfaction are different signals, and engagement only measures one of them.

A team led by Smitha Milli tested this directly. In February 2023 they recruited 806 Twitter users and compared the tweets the engagement-based algorithm showed each person with what a plain newest-first timeline would have shown. Participants then rated the tweets. The algorithmic feed carried noticeably more anger. Anger expressed by tweet authors was about half a standard deviation higher, and readers reported feeling angrier too. (A standard deviation is a measure of how spread out a set of scores is; half of one is a moderate effect, easily big enough to change the mood of a feed.) For political tweets the gap was even larger.

Here's the part that should stick. Users said they did not prefer the political tweets the algorithm picked for them. The system was serving content people engaged with but wouldn't have chosen. That isn't a conspiracy. Anger is engaging. It makes people reply, and on that 2023 price list a reply was worth 27 likes. The algorithm did exactly what it was told.

Economists have names for the gap. *Revealed preferences* are what your behavior shows you want. *Stated preferences* are what you say you want when someone asks you calmly. Feeds are built almost entirely on the first kind, because it's abundant, automatic and cheap to collect. The second kind takes asking, and asking is slow.

There's an old warning in economics, usually credited to Charles Goodhart: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Watch time and replies started out as decent clues that people were enjoying themselves. Turn them into the thing a billion-dollar system maximizes, and the system will find every way to raise the number, including ways that have nothing to do with enjoyment.

blocks.title: Two versions of you

left.head: What the model can see
items: You watched 90 percent of it
You replied within seconds
You stopped scrolling for eight seconds
You came back an hour later

right.head: What it can't see
items: You were annoyed the whole time
You were arguing, not enjoying
You were half asleep
You wish you'd gone to bed

blocks.text: It's worth being fair, too. Recommenders solve a real problem. Netflix's own research found that a typical member loses interest after 60 to 90 seconds of browsing, having looked at maybe 10 to 20 titles. Without a recommender, most of a giant library would be invisible, and plenty of great small creators would never be found. The issue isn't recommendation itself. It's what the system is told to maximize.
A feed is a mirror that reflects what you do, never what you meant. If you want it to show you something different, the only language it understands is behavior.
Taking back the controls

Once you see the machine as a behavior predictor wrapped in a weighting formula, the defensive moves become obvious. The model can't hear your intentions. It can only count your actions. So make your actions say what you mean.

items: Don't hate-watch. Lingering on rage bait is a vote for more of it, even if you never tap anything.
Use the negative buttons. 'Not interested' and 'don't recommend this channel' exist, and the published Twitter weights show how heavily negative feedback can count.
Search on purpose. A deliberate search hands the model a clear signal about what you want.
Finish what you value and bail fast on what you don't. Completion is one of the strongest signals platforms use.
Lean on subscription or following feeds when you can; they sit closer to your stated preferences.
Prune or pause your watch history if a binge has skewed things.

blocks.text: There's one more lever, and most people never get it: real time away. Months underway with no connection means you come back to apps running on an old picture of you. The first sessions back in port are fresh evidence. Spend them deliberately, and you're giving the model a new first draft instead of letting your most bored hours write it.

The deeper reframe is this. A feed isn't showing you what you like. It's showing you what a model predicted you would do, weighted by what a company decided to count. Once you see that, the scroll stops looking like a window onto the world. It's a very good guess about you, assembled as easily from your worst five minutes as from your best.

takeaways: Recommenders predict your actions, then rank by a formula that people chose. The formula defines what 'good' means.
On Twitter's published 2023 weights, a reply was worth 27 likes, which is one reason arguments travel so well.
Engagement measures what you do, not whether you're glad you did it.
Every linger, rewatch and reply is training data; deliberate searches and 'not interested' clicks are strong signals too.
Coming back online after time away is a chance to retrain your feed on purpose.

title: Five Half-Built Games Are Worth Zero
dek: Starting a project is the most fun you will ever have with it. That is exactly why serial starters end up with nothing, and why the fix is a rule, not more willpower.

blocks.text: Open almost any young developer's old hard drive and you will find a cemetery. A folder called *rpg_test*. Another called *new_idea_FINAL_v2*. A map with a lighthouse and no enemies, a dragon that flies beautifully but has nothing to fight, a slick menu screen for a game that never got a second level. Every one of those folders was born on a great night, the kind where a new idea felt so obviously better that the current project suddenly looked tired.

Here is the uncomfortable math. A player cannot play 80% of a game. A viewer cannot watch 80% of a video that was never uploaded. A customer cannot buy from 80% of a store. To the outside world, five projects that are each four-fifths done are worth exactly the same as zero projects. The hours were real and the skills you picked up were real, but the *value* only shows up at the finish line, and it shows up all at once.

That is why focus is not a productivity tip for a small builder. When you have a few hours a week, a partner with his own job, and long stretches where you cannot touch the project at all, focus is the entire strategy. Everything else in this library, from retention to moats, assumes you have something finished enough for real people to use.
The finish line is where the value lives

Programmers have an old joke, usually credited to Tom Cargill at Bell Labs: the first 90% of a project takes the first 90% of the time, and the last 10% takes the other 90%. It is funny because it is true, and it is true because of *what* lives in that last stretch. It is the tutorial that gets a confused stranger to the fun. The bug that only shows up with twelve players in a server. The thumbnail, the title, the game icon, the settings menu, the save system that does not wipe progress. Nobody dreams about these parts. They are also exactly the parts that decide whether a stranger stays or leaves in the first minute.

This creates a nasty asymmetry in how a project feels. Starting pays you immediately: every hour produces something visible and new, and every problem is still hypothetical. Finishing pays you almost nothing until release day: the hours go into invisible fixes, the problems are now real, and the design choices you made months ago are locked in. Your brain is not broken for preferring the first one. It is responding sensibly to the rewards in front of it. The trouble is that the rewards in front of you are not the rewards that matter.

blocks.title: Why starting always feels better than finishing

left.head: Starting a project
items: Everything is still possible
Fast, visible progress every session
Problems are hypothetical
Feels like momentum
Earns nothing from players

right.head: Finishing a project
items: Choices are locked in
Slow, invisible fixes
Every problem is real and yours
Feels like grinding
The only part players ever see

blocks.text: The price tag you never see

Economists call the real cost of any choice its *opportunity cost*: whatever else you would have done with the same time or money. Everyone learns the definition. Almost nobody uses it in the moment. In 2009, Shane Frederick and colleagues showed how easily people skip it with a tiny experiment. Students were asked whether they would buy a video of a favorite actor for $14.99. Half chose between buying it and simply not buying it. The other half got the same choice, except the second option was worded as keeping the $14.99 for other purchases.

Nothing about the deal changed. The money was always going to be available for other things. But spelling that out moved behavior by about 20 percentage points. People were not weighing the alternative until someone put it in front of them.

blocks.title: Students who chose to buy a $14.99 video
blocks.note: Same video, same price. Only the wording of the alternative changed (75 students per group).
blocks.source: Frederick et al., Journal of Consumer Research, 2009 (Study 1a data via OpenIntro)

blocks.text: New project ideas exploit the same blind spot. When an exciting idea shows up, you compare it to the current project's *problems*, not to the current project's *finish*. The new idea has no bugs yet, so it wins. But the honest price of the new idea is not zero. For a two-person team working in scraps of free time, its price is something like: the current game does not ship this year. Said out loud, that trade is often a bad one. It just never gets said out loud.

A practical habit follows directly from the study. Whenever one of you pitches a new direction, the other asks a single question: *instead of what?* If the answer is that the current game will wait three more months, you are at least now making the real decision instead of the fake one.
What Apple learned by cutting 70% of everything

When Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company was making a sprawling list of products: many overlapping Macintosh models, printers, the Newton handheld, and software lines that confused even employees. Jobs cut more than 70% of Apple's hardware and software products. He replaced the lineup with a simple grid of four: a consumer desktop, a consumer laptop, a pro desktop and a pro laptop. If a product did not fit one of those four boxes, it was gone.

items.label: Share of Apple's hardware and software products cut after Jobs returned
Apple's loss in fiscal 1997
Apple's profit in fiscal 1998

blocks.source: Macworld, Steve Jobs's seven key decisions; CNN Money, Oct 1998

blocks.text: Be careful with the lesson. Cutting products did not magically create a profit. What it did was free up engineers, money and attention so the company could make a few things well, including the iMac, instead of many things badly. The cuts also had a human cost: thousands of layoffs. Focus is not free. It means saying no to things that are genuinely good, and sometimes to people you like.

A tiny team faces the same trade on a smaller scale. Two people cannot run a Roblox game, a second game prototype, a YouTube channel and a store at the same time and do any of them well. Each one needs its own learning curve, its own audience and its own maintenance. Picking one does not mean the others are bad ideas. It means they are *later* ideas.

There is one useful exception: projects that feed each other instead of competing. A gaming channel that documents building the game, or a devlog that turns each update into a short video, is not really a second project. It is distribution for the first one, made from work you are already doing. The test is simple. If a side project uses the same hours to push the main project forward, it can stay. If it needs its own separate hours, its own audience and its own ideas, it goes in the parking lot until the main project ships.
Open loops are not free

Unfinished things also cost you when you are not working on them. Psychologists have long noticed that unfulfilled goals tend to keep popping back into the mind, an idea associated with Bluma Zeigarnik's work in the 1920s. In 2011, E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister ran experiments showing that an unfinished goal could interfere with an unrelated task, and that simply making a specific plan for the goal reduced that interference. You did not have to finish it. You had to decide what would happen to it.

Abandoned projects are the worst kind of open loop because they are never officially dead. The scrapped game sits in the back of your head as *maybe we'll go back to it*, quietly competing with the current one. Switching between projects has its own price too. The American Psychological Association's summary of task-switching research notes that each switch costs time, and that the cost grows when tasks are complex or unfamiliar. One researcher, David Meyer, has estimated that switching can eat up to 40% of productive time. That is an estimate, not a law of physics, but anyone who has reopened a project after a month away and spent the first hour just remembering how it works knows the feeling.
Quitting is not the enemy

None of this means you should never quit. The evidence actually points the other way. Economist Steven Levitt ran a large online experiment in which people stuck on a big decision, such as quitting a job, flipped a coin. Those whom the coin pushed toward making a change were more likely to make it, and they reported being happier six months later. His interpretation: people may be too cautious about big changes. Former poker professional Annie Duke makes a similar argument in her book *Quit*: most of us quit too late, because walking away feels like admitting failure.

So how do you square that with focus? The answer is that serial starters do not quit too much. They quit for the wrong reason, at the wrong time. They quit when the work gets boring, which happens around the middle of every project that has ever existed. They do not quit because they learned something, such as players trying the game and not coming back even after several rounds of fixes.
The test before you abandon anything: am I quitting because of something I *learned*, or because of something I *felt*? Evidence is a good reason to stop. Boredom at the 60% mark is just the middle.

Duke's best tool is the *kill criterion*: a signal, chosen in advance, that tells you to stop. You write it down at the start, while you are calm and not yet emotionally invested. A useful one has two parts, a date and a measurable condition. For a game, that might be a specific number of weeks after launch and a minimum share of new players who come back the next day. Pick your own numbers before you launch, because benchmarks vary a lot by genre and traffic source. The point is that the decision gets made by the plan you wrote when you were thinking clearly, not by the mood you are in at midnight after a frustrating bug.
A focus system for two people with almost no time

Limited time is not just a constraint here. It is a reason the rules have to be stricter. Someone working full time on a game can afford a week of wandering. Someone who gets a few free evenings between watches, then disappears underway for weeks, cannot. Every restart resets the clock on learning, testing and building an audience, and you have fewer clocks to spare than most people.

blocks.title: One active project, on purpose
items: Pick one active project. Every other idea goes in a written parking lot, not a new Studio file.
Define done as something strangers can touch: published, playable, with a first five minutes that works.
Set a ship date that fits your real hours, then cut features until the scope fits the date.
Write kill criteria now: a date plus a player-behavior number you choose before launch.
When a shiny idea shows up, park it and ask together: instead of what?
Finish or kill on purpose, then write a short close-out note so the loop actually closes.

blocks.text: The parking lot matters more than it sounds. Ideas are not the problem; partners who are excited about ideas are a good sign. Writing them down tells your brain they are safe and will not be lost, which is the Masicampo and Baumeister effect working for you. A good idea that waits six months is still a good idea. Many will look worse in six months, which is also useful information.

For a two-person team, the system also needs one agreement: neither of you can start a new project alone without the other's explicit yes. Most abandoned games die not in a big argument but in a slow drift, where one person starts tinkering with something new and the other quietly follows. Make the switch a decision, not an accident.

Long stretches away from the keyboard can even work in your favor. Time when you cannot build is good time for the parts that do not need a computer: sketching levels on paper, writing the parking lot, deciding what to cut, and listing the next three tasks so the first session back starts in motion instead of in confusion. Arriving with a plan turns a short window into real progress.
The person who finishes

There is a deeper reason to finish things, and it has little to do with any single game. Every finished project teaches you the parts that no unfinished project can: what launch day actually looks like, how strangers break your game in ways you never imagined, what the data says when real players vote with their time. The sixth time you start something, you mostly learn how to start. The first time you finish, you learn everything else.

That is the reframe worth keeping. Finishing is not just a result. It is a skill, built by repetition like any other, and like any skill it compounds. The builder who has shipped three small, imperfect games will usually make a better fourth game than the builder who has started twenty brilliant ones. Pick the project. Write the kill criteria. Then get it into strangers' hands.

takeaways: An unfinished project is worth zero to players; its value arrives only when it ships.
Every new idea has a hidden price: the current project not getting finished. Ask: instead of what?
Quit on evidence, not on boredom. Write kill criteria with a date and a number before you start.
Keep one active project and a written parking lot for everything else.
Close loops on purpose: finish or formally kill a project, then write it down.
