title: The Garden That Took Three Days
dek: One of the most-played games in history began as something a teenager threw together in a few days. The lesson is not luck. It is how fast you start learning.

blocks.text: On March 26, 2025, a 16-year-old Roblox developer going by BMWLux published a simple farming game. You planted seeds, waited, harvested, sold, bought better seeds. By the account of the studio that later joined the project, the original version took a few days to build. Nobody would have called it polished. A few weeks later it had around 500 people playing at once and somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 daily players: a solid little hit, nothing historic.

Then a studio called Splitting Point bought a share and did one thing relentlessly: it updated the game every week. Within about two weeks of their involvement, concurrent players hit roughly 100,000. Within about a month, a million. By late June, *Grow a Garden* had more than 21 million people playing at the same time, a figure the Associated Press reported as a record for any video game, beating the previous Fortnite high.

blocks.title: Grow a Garden peak concurrent players, 2025
blocks.note: Each record landed on an update or event day. The May 18 figure is approximate.
blocks.source: Wikipedia, Grow a Garden (compiling Roblox and press reports), 2026

blocks.text: It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this. The lesson is not that rushed games win. Thousands of quick Roblox games go nowhere, and you only hear about the ones that exploded, which is survivorship bias in its purest form. The real lesson is about *sequence*. The game got in front of players first and got good second, in public, one weekly update at a time. Every record in the chart above was set on an update or event day. The team was not guessing what players wanted. It was shipping, watching and shipping again.
You are worse at predicting players than you think

Why does shipping early beat polishing in private? Because almost nobody can predict what users will like, including professionals with enormous amounts of data. Ronny Kohavi, who ran Microsoft's experimentation platform, published a striking number in 2009. When Microsoft tested ideas in controlled experiments, ideas that someone had thought were worth building, only about a third improved the metric they were designed to improve. The rest did nothing or made things worse.

items.label: Microsoft ideas that improved the key metric they targeted when tested
Tested ideas that had no effect or hurt the metric

blocks.source: Kohavi et al., Online Experimentation at Microsoft, 2009

blocks.text: The same paper collects similar admissions from elsewhere: a Netflix figure that most of what the company tries turns out to be wrong, a lender's analyst who could guess test outcomes only about a third of the time. These are teams whose entire job is understanding users. If they are wrong two times out of three, two brothers designing a game at a kitchen table are not going to do better by thinking harder.

Once you accept that, the math of shipping changes. Every week you spend polishing an unreleased feature is a week spent betting on a guess that is probably wrong. Shipping early does not make your guesses better. It makes them *cheaper*, because you find out which ones are wrong before you have stacked a month of work on top of them.
Embarrassing is not the same as broken

LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman has a famous line, roughly: if the first version of your product does not embarrass you, you launched too late. It is good advice that is easy to misread. Embarrassing means *small*: placeholder art, one map, three upgrades, no trading system yet. It does not mean *broken*: crashes, a confusing first minute, a core loop that is not actually fun.

Roblox's own documentation draws the line clearly, even if it does not use those words. Its retention guide says the core loop and first-time experience drive whether players return the next day, and suggests getting players to the fun ideally in five minutes or less. Its discovery guide lists first-play bounce, players leaving within the first 60 seconds or within one to three minutes, among the most important signals its recommendation system watches. Rough edges are forgivable. A boring or confusing first minute is not.

blocks.title: What version 1 can and cannot get away with

left.head: Embarrassing: ship it
items: Placeholder or simple art
One map or one world
A handful of upgrades
No trading, guilds or events yet
A plain thumbnail you will redo

right.head: Broken: fix it first
items: Crashes or bad lag
Players unsure what to do
Core loop that is not fun yet
Progress that does not save
No reward in the first minutes

blocks.text: For a launcher-style obby, that might mean one world, one strong jump that feels great, a clear upgrade path for the first ten minutes, and nothing else. If the jump is fun and the first upgrade feels rewarding, players will forgive everything missing. If the jump feels floaty, no amount of extra worlds will save it, and you want to discover that in week three, not month eight.
Many cheap versions beat one perfect one

A small Stanford study adds an interesting twist on why iteration works. In 2010, Steven Dow and colleagues had 33 novice designers create web banner ads. Everyone made five drafts and got expert-style feedback, but one group made drafts in parallel, three at once and then two more, while the other group worked on one draft at a time. The final ads ran as a real campaign on a social network, so the researchers could measure what actual people clicked on.

blocks.title: Clicks per million ad views
blocks.note: Small study (33 novice designers). Parallel ads also got higher expert ratings.
blocks.source: Dow et al., ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 2010

blocks.text: The parallel group's ads got more clicks, higher expert ratings and longer visits from the people who clicked. The parallel designers also gained more confidence in their own design ability. It is one small study, so treat it as a clue rather than a law. But it points the same direction as everything else here: you learn more by putting several rough options in front of reality than by perfecting one in your head. For a game, that can be as simple as building two versions of the starting area and watching which one keeps playtesters around longer.
How Roblox actually tests your game

Shipping early matters even more on a platform that is itself running experiments on you. Roblox describes its Recommended for You system as a cycle of exploring and expanding. It shows a game to a small group of users who might like it. If that group engages, comes back and spends, it shows the game to more people like them. If they bounce, the expansion stalls.

blocks.title: The explore-and-expand loop
items: Roblox shows your game to a small group
Players engage, return or bounce
Signals are measured per player
Good signals: shown to more similar players
You update, and the loop runs again

blocks.text: One detail in the documentation is worth noticing. Roblox says the ranking signals are measured on players who arrived through the recommendation feed, averaged per player. In other words, the algorithm forms its opinion from strangers. That gives you a strong reason to put your game in front of strangers you can actually watch, such as a few people in a Discord or a playtest with friends of friends, before the algorithm's strangers arrive. Watching five real people play for ten minutes will tell you more than another month of building alone.
A shipping rhythm for a part-time team
Speed for a part-time team does not mean working faster. It means shortening the time between an idea and finding out whether it worked. Here is a rhythm that fits a few hours a week.

blocks.title: From idea to evidence, on repeat
items: Build version 0 in a few weekends: one core loop and a first five minutes that feels good.
Watch at least five people who are not you play it. Say nothing and take notes on where they get stuck.
Fix the biggest confusion, then publish. Do not wait for the features list to be complete.
Before each update, write down what you expect it to change, in one sentence.
Ship on a fixed rhythm. Roblox suggests smaller updates every two to four weeks.
Compare the result to your prediction, keep what worked, and cut what did not.

blocks.text: The written prediction is the step people skip, and it is the one that turns shipping into learning. Without it, every update feels like it went fine. With it, you start to notice how often your guesses miss, which is exactly the humility Kohavi's numbers suggest you need. If one partner is going to be unreachable for weeks, build updates in batches ahead of time so the other can release them on schedule. A rhythm that keeps running while you are away is worth more than a burst of work followed by silence.

There is a real cost to all this. Shipping early means strangers will see your worst work. Some will leave bad comments. A few will be right. That sting is the price of information, and it is far cheaper than the alternative: discovering after a year of private work that the thing you loved does not hold anyone's attention.
Shipping is where building starts

Most people treat release as the end of making a game. The *Grow a Garden* story suggests the opposite. The version that a teenager built in a few days was the beginning, the first question asked out loud. The game that broke records was the answer to hundreds of questions asked one update at a time.

That is the reframe worth keeping. Version 1 is not your best shot at success. It is your first chance to stop guessing. The embarrassment fades fast, and the learning compounds. The builders who win are rarely the ones with the best first draft. They are the ones who got to their tenth draft while everyone else was still polishing their first.

takeaways: Ship small, not broken: rough art is forgivable, a confusing first minute is not.
Even expert teams find that most of their ideas fail when tested, so make guesses cheap.
Watch real strangers play before the algorithm's strangers judge your game.
Write a one-sentence prediction before every update and check it afterward.
Release is not the finish line; it is the first time you stop guessing.

title: Why Good Practice Feels Like Losing
dek: Mixing up your practice makes you look worse while you train and better when it counts. The research on desirable difficulties explains why.

blocks.text: In a study published in 1994, a junior college baseball team agreed to an experiment. Thirty players were split into three groups. Ten got no extra practice. Ten got two extra batting sessions a week for six weeks, seeing 15 fastballs, then 15 curveballs, then 15 changeups, in neat blocks. The last ten got the same 45 pitches per session, but in random order, so they never knew what was coming next.

Anyone who has played sports can guess how the sessions felt. The blocked group got into a groove: by the tenth fastball in a row, you are timing it well. The random group kept getting fooled. Yet when everyone was tested at the end on randomly mixed pitches, like a real game, the random group had improved by about 57 percent from their starting level and the blocked group by about 25 percent. The group that looked worse at practice got better at baseball.

That pattern, where the practice that feels worse produces the learning that lasts, has a name. The UCLA psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork call it a *desirable difficulty*. Once you see it, you notice it everywhere, including in the way most people study for exams, train in games and learn to code.
Performance is not learning

The core idea is a distinction that sounds pedantic and turns out to be huge. Performance is what you can do right now, during practice. Learning is the lasting change that shows up later, in a different setting, after time has passed. You can watch performance. You can only infer learning, and the two often move in opposite directions.

Blocked practice is a performance-booster. When you do ten problems of the same type in a row, the method stays loaded in your head from one problem to the next, so you get them right and feel fluent. But that fluency is borrowed from the previous problem, not stored in long-term memory. Take away the crutch, by mixing types or adding a delay, and performance drops in practice. The Bjorks argue that this drop is often what drives durable learning, because it forces you to reconstruct the knowledge each time instead of coasting on what is already in your head.

In the Bjorks' framework, this is the gap between how accessible a memory is right now and how deeply it is stored. Easy practice inflates the first. Effortful practice, where you have to work to retrieve or reconstruct something, builds the second. Your feeling of mastery mostly reads the first, which is why it so often misleads you.

Their list of desirable difficulties is short: space your study sessions out instead of massing them, test yourself instead of rereading, interleave different topics instead of blocking them, and vary the conditions of practice. Spacing and testing each get their own article in this library. This one is about the less famous member of the family, interleaving, and about the crucial word in the phrase, *desirable*.
The math experiment

In 2007, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor at the University of South Florida taught college students to find the volume of four unusual solids, such as a wedge and a spheroid. Everyone did the same practice problems in two sessions. Blockers did all the wedge problems together, then all the spheroids, and so on. Mixers did the same problems shuffled. A week later, everyone took a test.

blocks.title: Blocked vs mixed math practice
blocks.note: Test given one week after the final practice session. Small study: 18 students completed it.
blocks.source: Rohrer & Taylor, Instructional Science, 2007

blocks.text: Practice scores made blocking look like the clear winner. Test scores told the opposite story, by a factor of three. The sample was small, just 18 students who finished all sessions, so treat the exact numbers with caution. But the reason for the reversal is the important part, and it generalizes.

When problems come in blocks, you never have to decide which method to use. The worksheet decides for you: it says Section 4.2 at the top. On a real test, or a real job, nobody tells you what kind of problem you are facing. Identifying the problem type is half the skill, and blocked practice skips it entirely. Mixed practice forces you to ask, every single time, what kind of problem this is and how you know.

There is a second, quieter benefit. Mixing problem types automatically spaces out each type, because between two wedge problems you do three others. Each time you return to a type, you have to pull the method back out of memory rather than reading it off the previous problem. So interleaving smuggles in both spacing and retrieval practice, which may be part of why its effects can be so large.
Blocked practice teaches you how to solve a problem once you know what it is. Interleaved practice teaches you to recognize what it is. Real life mostly tests the second.
From a lab to 787 students

Small lab studies are easy to dismiss, so Rohrer and his colleagues went big. In a randomized trial published in 2020, 54 seventh-grade math classes across five Florida schools used either mostly interleaved homework or the usual blocked kind for about four months. Both groups did the same problems, only in a different order. About a month after a review session, the students took an unannounced test.

items.label: Test scores, interleaved vs blocked homework, one month later
Effect size, which is large for a classroom study

blocks.source: Rohrer, Dedrick, Hartwig & Cheung, Journal of Educational Psychology, 2020

blocks.text: For an educational intervention that costs nothing but reshuffling homework, that is an unusually large effect. It is also one trial, in one subject and one age group, so the precise size should not be taken as a law of nature. But it shows the lab finding survives contact with real classrooms, real teachers and real teenagers.
The illusion that protects bad habits

If interleaving works so well, why does almost nobody do it on their own? Because it fools the people doing it. In a 2008 study, Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork had students learn the styles of 12 painters of landscapes and skies, from Georges Seurat to lesser-known artists, either seeing each artist's paintings in a block or mixed with the others. Later the students tried to identify the artists of new paintings they had never seen. Those who studied mixed paintings were right about 61 percent of the time on the first test block; those who studied in blocks managed about 35 percent.

Then the students were asked which method had worked better for them. Seventy-eight percent said blocking had been as good as or better than mixing, even though 78 percent had actually done better with mixing. They had just experienced the result and still believed the opposite. Blocked study felt like learning. Mixed study felt like confusion.

A second experiment in the same paper repeated the trick, with the same result. Of the students who expressed a preference, 64 out of 72 believed blocking had worked better. The bias was not a fluke of one group. It seems to be how people read their own learning.

This is the real obstacle. Your in-the-moment sense of progress is a performance meter, and desirable difficulties are designed to push that meter down. If you choose methods by how they feel, you will choose the wrong ones almost every time. That makes these techniques less a study tip and more a matter of trust: trusting evidence over your own feeling of fluency.

The same illusion traps teachers, coaches and training programs, not just learners. An instructor mostly sees performance during training: how smoothly the class works through problems, how many get the practice set right, how confident everyone looks at the end of the day. Every one of those signals rewards blocked, predictable, easy practice. Over time, curricula drift toward whatever makes training look good, which is not always what makes people good. Motor-learning researchers have studied this for decades under the name contextual interference, and the baseball study is one of its best-known demonstrations.
When difficulty is just difficulty

The word *desirable* is doing real work. The Bjorks are explicit that a difficulty helps only if you can respond to it successfully. If you lack the background knowledge to make sense of the challenge, it is not desirable, it is just hard. Shuffling problem types before you understand any of them produces confusion, not learning. Learn each method first, then mix.

The evidence also says interleaving is not universal. A 2019 meta-analysis by Brunmair and Richter pooled 238 effect sizes from 59 studies. Overall, interleaving beat blocking by a moderate margin, an effect size of 0.42. But it varied enormously. Paintings and other visual categories showed the biggest benefit, 0.67. Math showed a smaller benefit, 0.34. Results for expository texts were mixed, and for learning lists of words, blocking actually did better.

The pattern underneath was intuitive. Interleaving helped most when the categories were easy to confuse with each other, when the hard part was telling similar things apart. That is the situation where blocking hides the most and mixing reveals the most. When categories are already obviously different, there is little to gain.

It is also worth admitting how small some of the famous studies are. The baseball study had ten players per group, and the math study had 18 students. The large classroom trial and the meta-analysis are what make the overall picture credible, not any single striking chart.
Building difficulty into your practice

Technical training is full of easily confused categories, which is exactly where interleaving pays off. Electrical faults that present with similar indications. Thermodynamics problems that look alike but need different equations. Casualty procedures with overlapping symptoms. Bugs that throw similar errors for different reasons. In each case, the real skill is discrimination: noticing the one detail that tells you which situation you are in.

blocks.title: How to interleave without drowning
items: Learn each new method or system on its own first, until you can do a basic example.
Then build mixed practice sets: shuffle problem types so no two in a row need the same approach.
Before solving each one, say out loud which type it is and what tipped you off.
Mix in older material, not just this week's, so earlier topics stay in rotation.
Expect your practice scores to drop. Judge the method by delayed tests, not by how practice feels.

blocks.text: For a board or a big exam, that means quizzing across systems rather than finishing one system completely before touching the next. For math and physics, it means pulling problems from different chapters into one set rather than doing the end-of-section exercises in order. For coding, it means building small projects that need several concepts at once instead of drilling one concept per tutorial. For game skills, it is the same lesson as the batting cage: training against one predictable bot pattern feels great and transfers poorly to opponents who do not cooperate.

Interleaving also changes how you should read your own results. If you switch to mixed practice sets and your scores drop from 90 percent to 60, that does not mean the method failed. It means the old 90 was partly an illusion created by the format. The fair comparison is how you do on a mixed, delayed test, the kind you will face on a board or in a real casualty, and on that measure the 60 is the more honest number and the one that climbs.

Varying conditions counts too. Practicing a procedure only at one panel, in one order, with one instructor watching, builds a skill tied to that setting. Changing the setup, the order of questions, or the person quizzing you makes your knowledge less dependent on any single set of cues.

blocks.title: Same problems, different order

left.head: Blocked
items: Ten of one type, then ten of the next
Method stays loaded between problems
High practice scores, smooth feeling
Weak at telling problem types apart

right.head: Interleaved
items: Types shuffled, no two alike in a row
Must choose the method every time
Lower practice scores, feels messy
Builds recognition of what you are facing

blocks.text: If you doubt all this, test it on yourself. Next time you have two similar topics to learn, practice one in blocks and the other mixed with older material, and quiz yourself on both a week later without warning. Personal experiments are not science, but they are a good way to stop trusting the feeling and start trusting the result.

The hardest thing about desirable difficulties is not using them. It is tolerating how they feel. Every one of them makes you look worse in the short term, to yourself and to anyone watching. The payoff arrives later, quietly, when the pitch you were not expecting comes in, and you hit it anyway.

takeaways: How well you perform during practice is a poor guide to how much you are learning.
Mixing problem types forces you to identify the problem, which is half of real-world skill.
Learn each method first, then interleave; difficulty without background knowledge is just confusion.
Interleaving helps most when categories are easy to confuse, and can hurt for simple word lists.
Judge study methods by delayed tests, not by how smooth practice feels.

title: The Test Is the Lesson
dek: Rereading feels like studying. Pulling information out of your own head, even badly, is what actually makes it stick.

blocks.text: In an experiment at Washington University in St. Louis, a group of undergraduates sat down with a short science passage, a few hundred words about the sun or about sea otters. Some read it four times. Others read it once and then spent the remaining sessions trying to write down everything they could remember, with no feedback and no peeking. The first group saw the text about 14 times in total. The second group saw it about three and a half times.

Five minutes later, the readers won easily. One week later, the result had flipped: the students who had mostly tested themselves remembered half again as much as the students who had mostly reread. The experiment, published in 2006 by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, became one of the most cited demonstrations of what psychologists call the testing effect, or retrieval practice. Its message runs against almost every study habit people have: a test is not just a way to measure learning. Taking one is learning.
The scoreboard that flipped

The design was simple. In the second experiment, 180 students were split into three study schedules made of five-minute periods. One group studied the passage in all four periods (SSSS). One studied three times and took one recall test (SSST). One studied once and took three recall tests (STTT). Then each student took a final test, either five minutes later or a week later.

blocks.title: Share of the passage recalled one week later
blocks.note: At five minutes the order was reversed: 83%, 78% and 71%.
blocks.source: Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006

blocks.text: Look at the forgetting rates rather than the raw scores. Over the week, the reread-only group lost about 52 percent of what they had shown at the five-minute mark. The mostly-testing group lost about 14 percent. Rereading builds something that looks impressive right away and drains fast. Retrieval builds something that looks weaker at first and holds.

The first experiment in the same paper showed the same crossover with 120 students. Restudying was slightly ahead at five minutes, 81 percent to 75 percent. Two days later, testing led 68 to 54. After a week it led 56 to 42. If you only ever check your learning right after studying, you will reliably pick the wrong method.
Your confidence is lying to you

Here is the most uncomfortable detail. After the learning phase, the students rated how well they expected to remember the passage in a week on a scale of one to seven. The repeat-readers were the most confident, averaging 4.8. The repeat-testers were the least confident, at 4.0. The group that would do best felt worst about its chances, and the group that would do worst felt best.

The reason is fluency. When you reread something, it flows. The words are familiar, the diagram looks right, and your brain mistakes that ease for knowing. But recognizing an answer when it is in front of you is a different skill from producing it when it is not, and a qual board, a casualty and a coding interview all demand the second. Testing feels harder because it exposes the gaps, which is exactly why it is useful.

blocks.title: Two ways to spend the same hour

left.head: Rereading and highlighting
items: Feels smooth and productive
Builds recognition: I have seen this
Hides what you cannot produce
Strong at five minutes, fades fast

right.head: Retrieval practice
items: Feels slow and frustrating
Builds recall: I can produce this
Shows you exactly what is missing
Weaker at five minutes, lasts weeks

blocks.text: A 2008 study by Karpicke and Roediger in *Science* made the point with Swahili vocabulary. Students who kept being tested on words even after they had got them right recalled about 80 percent a week later. Students whose words were dropped from testing once they had recalled them, whether or not they kept restudying, managed only 33 to 36 percent. Once a word could be recalled, extra studying added little; extra retrieval added a lot. The students' own predictions of how they would do bore little relation to any of this.
Better than the fancy methods, too

Retrieval does not only beat passive rereading. In a 2011 study, also in *Science*, Karpicke and Janell Blunt compared it with concept mapping, a popular active technique where students draw diagrams connecting the main ideas. Eighty Purdue students read a passage about sea otters, then either stopped, reread it repeatedly, built a concept map, or practiced recalling it. A week later they took a test with both factual and inference questions.

blocks.title: Test score one week after studying a science text
blocks.source: Karpicke & Blunt, Science, 2011 (as summarized by the What Works Clearinghouse)

blocks.text: Retrieval won on the inference questions as well as the facts, which matters, because a common objection is that testing only builds parrot memory. A fair caveat, flagged by the US Department of Education's What Works Clearinghouse when it reviewed the study: the retrieval and concept-mapping groups spent more total time studying than the two reading groups, so the comparison with rereading is not perfectly clean. The head-to-head with concept mapping, at equal time, is the stronger result.

One more detail from that work is worth sitting with. Right after the learning session, students who practiced retrieval and students who mapped concepts could recall about the same amount. The difference only showed up a week later. Students also tended to overestimate how well they knew the material whenever it was sitting in front of them, which is precisely the condition rereading and concept mapping create. Methods that keep the source in view keep the illusion running.
How big is the effect, really?

Single studies can mislead, so the better question is what happens across many. In 2014, Christopher Rowland pooled 159 effect sizes from 61 studies comparing testing with restudying. The average advantage was an effect size of 0.50, which is moderate: large enough to move a typical student well up the class, not large enough to be magic. A 2013 review led by John Dunlosky rated ten common study techniques and gave its top rating, high utility, to only two: practice testing and spacing your study out. Rereading and highlighting were rated low.

items.label: Average effect size of testing over restudy when tests gave feedback
Average effect size without feedback

blocks.source: Rowland, Psychological Bulletin, 2014

blocks.text: The meta-analysis also found which details matter. Tests with feedback roughly doubled the benefit compared with tests without it. Recall tests, where you produce the answer, generally beat recognition tests like multiple choice. And the advantage was bigger when the final test came a day or more later rather than the same day, which is exactly when it matters.

There are real limits. Most of this research uses word lists, facts and short passages. In 2015, Tamara van Gog and John Sweller argued that the testing effect shrinks and may even disappear for highly complex material, where many elements must be understood together; other researchers dispute how far that goes, and the debate is not settled. And testing only works if you can retrieve something. Quizzing yourself on a chapter you never understood just produces blank pages; learn it first, then test.
Why pulling beats pushing

A useful mental model: memory is less like a hard drive and more like a trail through a forest. Reading the trail map does little to the trail. Walking it, especially when it is overgrown and you have to push through, wears it deeper. Every successful retrieval changes the memory itself, strengthening the routes you used and often linking the item to new cues. The effort is not a side effect; it is the work.

Testing also has an indirect benefit that is easy to overlook. It tells you, precisely, what you do not know. A reread chapter gives you a vague warm feeling about the whole thing. A blank page where the third interlock should be gives you a target. That is why good testing is followed by checking: retrieve, compare, fix the misses, and come back later to retrieve again.

Robert and Elizabeth Bjork at UCLA offer a sharper version of this idea. Every memory, they argue, has two separate strengths. Storage strength is how deeply it is embedded and connected to other knowledge. Retrieval strength is how easy it is to pull up right now. Rereading pumps up retrieval strength, which is why the material feels known, but does little for storage. Retrieving something when retrieval strength has dropped, when it takes effort to dig out, is what builds storage strength. The feeling of strain is the sensation of the deeper number going up.

That model also explains why cramming and rereading are so seductive. Your sense of how well you know something reads the retrieval-strength gauge, because that is the only one you can feel. The storage-strength gauge, the one that decides what you will know in a month, is invisible. You have to infer it from evidence, and the best evidence is a test taken after a delay.
If a study method lets you feel good without ever being wrong, it is probably not doing much. Productive studying includes a steady stream of small, private failures.
Turning it into a method
For technical material, retrieval practice can look like many things besides flashcards. The common thread is that the answer comes out of your head before you look at the source.

blocks.title: A retrieval session for technical material
items: Read or watch the material once, carefully, until it makes sense.
Close everything. Write or draw all you can: the system, the steps, the equations.
Check against the source and mark every miss and error in a different color.
Rework the misses from memory, not by copying them.
Come back in a few days and do the blank-page test again before reviewing.

blocks.text: For systems, sketch the line diagram from memory and label every valve and interlock you can, then compare. For procedures, recite the immediate actions in order before you open the book. For math and physics, do practice problems cold instead of rereading worked examples, and only look at the solution after a real attempt. For coding, close the tutorial and rebuild the feature from a blank file; the errors you hit are the lesson. For game design, explain a mechanic to a friend without your notes.

Format matters less than effort, but a few rules hold up. Producing an answer beats picking one, so prefer blank-page questions over multiple choice when you can. Always check your answer afterward, since feedback was the biggest single booster in the meta-analysis. And once you can retrieve something, do not retire it. The Swahili study showed that dropping items from testing as soon as you get them right throws away most of the benefit. Instead, push them further out and test them again later, which is where retrieval practice and spacing become the same habit.

Nuclear training already contains a version of this, whether or not anyone calls it that. Boards, walkthroughs and oral checkouts force you to produce knowledge on demand, out loud, under mild pressure. That is retrieval practice with feedback built in. The trap is the preparation for them: hours of rereading notes and highlighting the manual, which feels like getting ready and is mostly not. Swap half of that time for self-quizzing and the board itself becomes less of a shock, because you have already been doing the thing it measures.

The same goes for anything you are learning on your own time. A tutorial you follow line by line is rereading with extra steps. You get the warm feeling of progress, and a week later you cannot start the project without it open. The fix costs nothing: after each lesson, shut it, open a blank file, and try to build the thing again. You will get stuck within minutes. Getting unstuck, with the tutorial as a last resort instead of a first, is the moment the knowledge actually moves into your head.

Study partners help if you use them right. Quizzing each other before a board is retrieval practice with built-in feedback. Listening to someone else explain the system is mostly rereading with a voice.

The hardest part is psychological. Retrieval practice will make you feel less prepared than rereading, right up until the moment it counts. The students in 2006 who did best were the ones who felt worst about it. Learning to trust that feeling of strain, instead of chasing the comfort of familiarity, may be the single most valuable study skill there is.

takeaways: Closing the book and recalling beats rereading for anything you need to remember beyond tomorrow.
Your confidence after rereading is a poor predictor; the method that feels worse often works better.
Check your answers. Feedback roughly doubled the benefit of testing in the 2014 meta-analysis.
Produce answers (draw, write, recite, code) rather than just recognizing them.
Understand material first, then test it; quizzing yourself on what you never learned only yields blanks.

title: Forgetting Is Part of the Plan
dek: A 140-year-old self-experiment and a 1,354-person study agree: when you review matters almost as much as whether you review.

blocks.text: Picture two sailors with the same qual card and the same five weeks before the board. The first coasts for a month, then spends the last three nights grinding the material for hours. The second does short sessions spread across all five weeks and comes back to each system only after he has half-forgotten it. On board day they may score about the same. Ask them the same questions six months later, mid-deployment, when a drill actually needs that knowledge, and the difference between them is enormous.

The second sailor is using one of the oldest and most replicated findings in psychology: the spacing effect. It has been known since the 1880s, confirmed in hundreds of experiments, and almost everyone still studies as if it did not exist. Why that happens is the interesting part, because it reveals how poorly the feeling of *I know this* predicts what you will actually remember.
The man who memorized nonsense

In the early 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus ran what may be the most tedious experiment in the history of science, with himself as the only subject. He memorized lists of meaningless syllables, chosen precisely because they gave his mind nothing to hook onto. In his main series each list had 13 syllables. He drilled a list until he could recite it without error, waited a set amount of time, and then measured how long it took him to learn it again.

That last step was the clever part. Instead of asking how much he could still recall, he measured *savings*: the share of the original learning time he no longer needed. If a list took 1,000 seconds to learn and 600 seconds to relearn, the savings was 40 percent. The method could detect memories too faint to produce a single recalled syllable, because even a faint trace makes relearning faster.

blocks.title: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve
blocks.note: Savings = how much less time relearning took than the original learning.
blocks.source: Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (1885; English trans. 1913)

blocks.text: The shape is the famous forgetting curve. Most of the loss happens fast: within an hour, more than half of the benefit of his original effort was gone. Then the curve flattens. A month later he still kept about a fifth of the savings, and that remnant was fading only slowly. In 2015, Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros at the University of Amsterdam redid the experiment with a single subject, Dros himself, over roughly 70 hours. The new curve closely resembled the original, with one odd bump: memory looked slightly better at the 24-hour mark than the trend predicted, which the authors tentatively linked to sleep.

Notice what the curve actually says, because it gets misquoted constantly. It does not say you lose everything. It says that material studied once and never touched again leaks away fast and then settles into a thin, durable residue. It also says something hopeful: even after you feel you have forgotten, relearning is cheaper than learning. The trace is still in there. The real question is how to make it thicker each time you come back to it.
Half the work, same result

Ebbinghaus also noticed that repetitions spread across several days did more for him than the same number crammed into one sitting. That observation became the spacing effect, and it has been tested exhaustively since. A 2006 review by Nicholas Cepeda, Harold Pashler and colleagues pooled 839 assessments from 317 experiments in 184 articles. Spaced practice beat massed practice for verbal recall, and the best gap between sessions grew as the time you need to remember grew.

One of the most striking demonstrations came from four psychologists who all shared the surname Bahrick. Over nine years they learned and relearned 300 foreign-language word pairs, then tested themselves up to five years after training ended. Thirteen sessions spaced 56 days apart produced retention similar to 26 sessions spaced 14 days apart. Wider spacing bought the same memory for half the sessions. With only four subjects it is a vivid case study rather than proof, which is why the big controlled experiments matter.

Spacing is not just for vocabulary. In a 2007 study, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor taught college students a type of math problem and gave them the same practice problems either in one block or split across two sessions a week apart. During practice the two groups performed almost identically. On a test a week later, the spacers scored 74 percent and the massers 49 percent. The extra practice the massers did in a single sitting added almost nothing; a third group that did less massed practice scored about the same as them.
The ridgeline: how long to wait

The most useful of those experiments was published in 2008 by Cepeda, Ed Vul, Doug Rohrer, John Wixted and Pashler. They recruited 1,354 people online and had them learn 32 obscure but true trivia facts, the kind of thing you would never already know. Each person reviewed the facts once after a gap ranging from zero to 105 days, then took a final test after a retention interval of 7, 35, 70 or 350 days. Every person got exactly the same amount of study; only the timing changed.

Two results stood out. First, the payoff from spacing was large. For people tested a year later, reviewing at the best gap improved recall by 77 percent compared with reviewing immediately, and at the 70-day test the improvement was 111 percent. Second, the best gap was not a fixed number. It depended on how long you needed to remember, and as a fraction of that time it shrank.

blocks.title: Best review gap as a share of how long you need to remember
blocks.note: Estimated optimal gap for recall: about 3, 8, 12 and 27 days respectively.
blocks.source: Cepeda et al., Psychological Science, 2008

blocks.text: Translate that into your calendar. If the board is a week out, review a few days after you first learn something. If it is five weeks out, wait about a week. If you want to still know it a year from now, as in when you are standing a watch and the indication in front of you is not in the book, the ideal second look comes three or four weeks later. The authors called the pattern a temporal ridgeline: a ridge of best gaps that climbs as the target date moves further away.

There is a forgiving detail buried in the data. Retention climbed steeply as the gap grew toward the optimum and then declined only gradually past it. In the authors' words, the cost of a too-long gap was much smaller than the cost of using too short a gap. If you are unsure, err late. Reviewing the same evening feels productive and is the least useful choice of all.

items.label: Better recall after a year when the review came at the best gap instead of right away
People in the 2008 spacing study

blocks.source: Cepeda et al., Psychological Science, 2008

blocks.text: Why spacing works, and why it feels wrong

Researchers still argue about the mechanism. One leading idea is that a review helps most when the memory has partly faded, so retrieving it takes real effort, and that effort strengthens it more than an easy repeat would. Another says that studying at different times attaches the memory to more varied contexts and cues, giving you more routes back to it later. A third says that a second pass right after the first gets lazy processing because the material still feels fresh. These ideas are not mutually exclusive, and the honest answer is that the effect is far better established than its explanation.

Whatever the cause, spacing has a public relations problem. Cramming produces a feeling of mastery that is real, just short-lived. Spaced review feels worse in the moment because each time you return, you have forgotten some of it and have to struggle. That struggle is the point, but your brain reads it as failure. The psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork have a name for this, desirable difficulties, and it is a big enough idea to deserve its own article.
The moment you feel a little rusty on something is not a sign that you studied it wrong. It is usually the best time to review it.

Schools make this worse by rewarding the short game. Unit tests reward cramming, and then the material is never examined again. Nuclear training is unusual because it keeps coming back: the facts from power school show up on boards, in quals, in drills and in real casualties years later. That is exactly the situation where the ridgeline says spacing pays off most.

The best part is that spacing is close to free. In the 2008 study, every group got identical study time; the only variable was the calendar. In the Bahrick study, wider gaps actually cut the number of sessions in half. You do not need more hours to benefit. You need to take the hours you were going to spend anyway and stop stacking them on the same night. For someone whose free time comes in scattered chunks between watches, that is good news: scattered is exactly the right shape.
Building a spacing habit for technical material

Flashcard software built on spaced repetition, such as Anki, automates the ridgeline. Each time you answer a card correctly, its next appearance is pushed further out, so cards you know well show up rarely and shaky ones keep coming back. It runs offline on a phone, which matters on a submarine. It is ideal for crisp facts: setpoints, alarm meanings, component names, formulas, the steps of a procedure in order.

It has limits worth respecting. The big studies used word pairs and trivia, and spacing evidence is thinnest for deep conceptual understanding. A card that asks you to recite a number teaches you the number, not why the system behaves the way it does. For systems knowledge, space bigger units: redraw a system from memory every couple of weeks, rework a problem set you did a month ago, or explain a casualty response out loud without notes. The same logic applies when learning to code: rebuild a small feature from scratch a week after the tutorial instead of rereading it.

Card design decides whether the app helps or just feels busy. Keep each card to one fact, phrase it as a question you must answer before flipping, and actually say or write the answer rather than nodding at it. Make cards from material you already understand; a card can preserve knowledge, but it is a poor way to acquire it. And prune ruthlessly. A deck of a few hundred cards you review daily beats a deck of five thousand you abandon in week three.

You may hear arguments about whether gaps should expand (one day, then three, then ten) or stay equal. Expanding schedules are what most software uses and they are convenient, but the research comparing them to equal spacing is mixed, and some studies found equal gaps held up as well or better over the long run. The big, reliable effect is spacing versus cramming. The fine-tuning matters much less than simply coming back.

blocks.title: A spaced plan for one qual system
items: Day 0: learn it properly, then close the book and write down what you remember.
Day 1 or 2: redraw the system and list its interlocks from memory, then check.
About one week: answer practice board questions cold, no peeking first.
About three to four weeks: explain the whole system out loud, including casualties.
After that: put the facts you keep missing into flashcards and let the app space them.

blocks.text: Two practical rules make this survivable on a busy watch rotation. Keep sessions short, because spacing works with many short visits rather than a few heroic ones. And when you miss days, do not try to catch up all at once; just restart the queue. A slightly late review costs little, as the 2008 data showed.

The deeper lesson is about trusting the right signal. Your sense of fluency in the moment is a measure of how recently you saw something, not how well you will know it later. Ebbinghaus showed that forgetting is fast and that it never quite reaches zero. Spacing turns that leftover trace into the foundation of the next session. Forgetting, used well, is not the opposite of learning. It is part of the mechanism.

takeaways: Forgetting is steep at first, then flattens; what is left makes relearning cheaper.
Space reviews at roughly 10 to 20 percent of how long you need to remember something.
When unsure, review later rather than sooner; too short a gap costs far more than too long.
Use spaced flashcards for facts, and spaced redraws or re-explanations for whole systems.
Feeling rusty at a review is a feature, not a sign you studied wrong.
